question_text: A recently married young lady has missed her periods. Her pregnancy is confirmed with urine pregnancy test. She is 8 weeks pregnant and has come to see you with complaints of incessant vomiting. She is dehydrated.

sub_questions.text: What are the differential diagnosis for the vomiting? [2]
answer: Hyperemesis Gravidarum - severe, persistent vomiting leading to dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.
Gastrointestinal disorders - e.g., gastritis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, gastroenteritis, peptic ulcer, cholecystitis, UTI, pyelonephritis.
Diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperthyroidism
Twisted ovarian tumor, red degeneration of fibroid
Psychogenic

sub_questions.text: How will you manage excessive vomiting in the first trimester of pregnancy? [4]
answer: Clinical evaluation - onset, duration and extent of vomiting. Associated weight loss, associated decrease in appetite. Diet and hydration status

Lab investigations - Serial B HCG levels to rule out molar pregnancy, CBC- rule out anemia and infective cause. Serum electrolyte, blood sugar levels, TSH, urine ketone, USG - ANC scan- for the viability of the fetus
Hydration and electrolyte correction - Oral rehydration if mild; IV fluids (normal saline or Ringer lactate) if dehydrated-moderate to severe case of HG.

Antiemetics - e.g., doxylamine (25mg) - pyridoxine (25mg) combination, promethazine (12.5mg -25mg), cyclizine 50mg, prochlorperazine 5-10mg, ondansetron 4-8mg, domperidone 10mg, metochlorpramide 5-10mg.
Nutritional support - Small frequent meals, dry foods; if oral intake fails, consider nasogastric feeding or TPN in extreme cases.
Monitor and correct metabolic disturbances - Check for ketonuria, hypokalemia, and liver function abnormalities; correct as needed.
IV/oral thiamine - if severe starvation/vomiting
Psychogenic counselling
*treatment can range from OPD management (ORS+ diet change) to IPD admission and rigorous hydration depending on the patient's condition*

sub_questions.text: What are the conditions that need to be ruled out in this patient with excessive vomiting in the first trimester of pregnancy? [2]
answer: Molar pregnancy (Hydatidiform mole) - Suspect with excessive symptoms, larger uterine size, and very high β-hCG.
Multiple pregnancy - Higher hormone levels may cause more severe vomiting.
Ectopic Pregnancy

sub_questions.text: What are the indications for admission and referral? [2]
answer: Persistent vomiting with dehydration and ketonuria despite outpatient treatment.
Electrolyte imbalance, weight loss >5%, or suspicion of underlying complications (e.g., molar pregnancy or liver dysfunction).
Possible Complications of HG- esophageal tears/ AKI/ prolonged depression/ thiamine deficiency/ vitamin K deficiency

question_text: A 25-year-old lady, married for one year, has come to see you after she missed her regular periods; Her pregnancy was confirmed with urine pregnancy test and she was prescribed folic acid. Today, she reports two months amenorrhea and having bleeding PV since one hour ago.

sub_questions.text: What are the causes of bleeding PV in the first trimester of pregnancy? [4]
answer: Implantation bleed- 6-12 days after conception- physiological
Threatened abortion - Bleeding with a closed cervical os and viable intrauterine pregnancy.
Inevitable/incomplete/complete/spontaneous abortion - Bleeding with open os and partial or complete expulsion of products.
Ectopic pregnancy - Implantation outside the uterine cavity, often associated with pain and minimal bleeding.
Molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole) - Abnormal trophoblastic proliferation with excessive β-hCG, vaginal bleeding, and uterine enlargement
Subchorionic hematoma- accumulation of blood between uterine wall and chorionic membrane- light to heavy bleed
Others- cervical/vaginal infections/ physiological change of cervix can cause spotting

sub_questions.text: Draw an algorithm for management of bleeding PV in the first trimester of pregnancy. [6]

algorithm: Patient presents with bleeding PV in first trimester

Take history and perform physical exam (pain, amount of bleeding, Onset, duration and progress, h/o previous pregnancies, bad obstetric history, rule out systemic cause of bleed/ dizziness/ passage of tissue)
Check vitals → If unstable: resuscitate immediately
Perform pelvic exam (speculum + bimanual- check cervical changes and signs of infection Cervical os- opened or closed Uterine size, adnexal tenderness and presence of mass/lesion)
Labs- Serial HCG/ UPT/CBC/ urine routine/blood grouping and cross matching/TSH/BSL/iron studies/serology
Do transvaginal ultrasound/ USG + Serum β-hCG
Viable intrauterine pregnancy                        No intrauterine pregnancy or Product of concepton-inevitable/complete
Threatened abortion                                 Rule out ectopic pregnancy
If bleeding worsen                                  If ectopic confirmed- medical Mx Surgery
If nonviable pregnancy or molar pregnancy confirmed

question_text: A 25-year-old PRIMI at 40+4 weeks of GA is admitted for safe confinement. She is in the second stage of labour and she looks exhausted. You would like to cut short second stage of labour.

sub_questions.text: What are the indications for cutting short of second stage of labour? [3]
answer: Maternal exhaustion or distress causing maternal instability - As in this case, the mother is unable to push effectively.
Obstetric Emergency- placental abruption/ fetal compromise/ uterine rupture
Fetal distress - Abnormal fetal heart rate suggesting hypoxia (e.g., late decelerations, bradycardia)/ abnormal CTG readings
Hypertensive disorder of pregnancy
Prolonged second stage - 2 hours in a nulliparous woman (or >3 hours with epidural) or 1 hour in a multiparous woman (or >2 hours with epidural)

sub_questions.text: What are the instruments used to cut short the second stage of labour? [4]
answer: Vacuum extractor (Ventouse) - Applied to fetal scalp to assist with delivery.
Forceps - Types include outlet forceps, low-cavity forceps (e.g., Wrigley's, Simpson's).
Episiotomy scissors - To enlarge vaginal outlet if needed.
Delivery forceps for breech extraction (e.g., Piper's forceps) - in specific malpresentations.

sub_questions.text: What are the complications anticipated and how will you manage them? [3]

answer.management: Prompt Repair With Sutures Under Asepsis

answer.complication: Postpartum Hemorrhage (PPH) Due To Trauma Or Atony
answer.management: Uterotonics (E.G., Oxytocin), Uterine Massage, IV Fluids, Blood Transfusion If Needed, Tamponade, B-Lynch Suturing As Per The Status /Severity

answer.complication: Neonatal Injury (E.G., Scalp Laceration, Cephalohematoma With Vacuum; Facial Nerve/ Brachial plexus Injury With Forceps)
answer.management: Neonatal Monitoring, Imaging If Needed, Supportive Care, Immediate Surgery if severe

answer.complication: Urinary And Anorectal Problem- Bladder/Urethral Injury
answer.management: Counselling and surgical repair if needed

question_text: A 30-year-old pregnant lady G5P4L4 at 32 weeks of pregnancy has come for routine antenatal visit to the community health center. Her hemoglobin is 8 gm%,

sub_questions.text: List the factors contributing to the anemia in pregnancy. [2]
answer: Increased iron demand during pregnancy (especially in multigravida like G5P4L4).
Nutritional deficiencies - Iron, folic acid, and vitamin B12 deficiency.
Diminished absorption - due to loss of acidic environment in duodenum because of excessive use of antacids .PPI.
Infections - e.g., malaria, hookworm infestation, chronic urinary tract infections.
Short inter-pregnancy interval - Depletes maternal iron stores due to repeated pregnancies.
Chronic blood loss - through GI tract or heavy menstrual bleeding
Already anemic in pre-pregnancy state.

sub_questions.text: How will you manage anemia in this pregnancy? [4]
answer: History and clinical examination- fatigue/pale skin/pallor/SOB/ dizziness/ lightheadedness/cold extremities/ tachycardia

Confirm diagnosis and type of anemia - CBC with Peripheral smear, serum iron studies with ferritin, MCV/MCH for classification (microcytic, macrocytic, etc.)/LDH/ Vit B12/D3 urine routine/ stool routine and occult blood, LFT, USG abdomen and pelvis
Oral iron therapy (if tolerated and compliant) - Elemental iron 100-200 mg/day + folic acid e.g. ferrous sulphate (325mg), ferrous fumarate (200mg), ferrous gluconate (300mg)

Parenteral iron therapy (if poor response to oral iron or moderate anemia late in pregnancy) - IV iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose is preferred. Calculate total dose required using body weight and Hb deficit: Iron requirement = 2.21 x body weight x (target Hb - patient Hb) + 1000 mg
Dietary counseling - Iron-rich foods (green leafy vegetables, jaggery, liver, meat), Advise to avoid tea/coffee near meals and take iron with vitamin C for better absorption
Deworming (Albendazole after 1st trimester) if needed

sub_questions.text: What are the precautions need to be taken during the delivery and puerperium? [4]
answer: Prepare for postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) - Active management of third stage of labour (AMTSL), ensure uterotonics available
Monitor for signs of decompensation - Tachycardia, breathlessness, fatigue - especially during labor and early puerperium
Continue iron and folic acid supplementation in puerperium for at least 3 months
Iron rich diet/ vit C rich food/ avoid iron inhibitors/ regular ANC checkup/ screening/ adequate hydration
Educate on contraception and birth spacing - Prevent recurrent anemia due to frequent pregnancies, Counsel for postpartum IUCD or sterilization if family is complete

question_text: A young couple married for 4 years and living together and anxious to conceive. They have come to the family physician for the infertility evaluation.

sub_questions.text: Define primary infertility. [2]
sub_questions.answer: Primary infertility is defined as the inability to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected sexual intercourse, without ever having conceived previously.

sub_questions.text: How will you evaluate a couple for infertility in primary care? [4]
answer: History-taking (both partners): Duration and frequency of cohabitation and intercourse, Menstrual history: regularity, flow, dysmenorrhea, or signs of ovulation, Past medical/surgical history, STIs, tuberculosis, or pelvic infections(PID), Lifestyle factors: smoking, alcohol, stress, weight changes, Sexual dysfunction or ejaculation issues in male partner, MTP/abortions---inflammation-- tubal blockage, Use of OCPS

Physical examination: Female: BMI, thyroid, signs of PCOS, pelvic examination for uterine/adnexal abnormalities, Male: Secondary sexual characteristics, genital exam for varicocele, undescended testes
Basic investigations: Female: Day 2-3 FSH, LH, TSH, prolactin, pelvic ultrasound (to assess uterus and ovaries), Follicular studies, Male: Semen analysis (after 2-7 days abstinence)
Counseling and emotional support - Address stress, expectations, and provide reassurance

sub_questions.text: What are the simple treatment measures that can be tried in the family practice before we refer to the specialist? [4]
answer: Lifestyle modifications: Weight optimization (especially in PCOS or obese women), Avoid smoking, alcohol, and stress management
Timed intercourse advice: how to track ovulation (calendar method, cervical mucus, ovulation kits), Advise intercourse every alternate day during fertile window (days 10-18 in 28-day cycle)
Nutritional support and supplements: Folic acid for female, multivitamins for both partners, Treat anemia, hypothyroidism, or hyperprolactinemia if present

Empirical ovulation induction (if anovulation suspected and investigations support it) with follicular studies for timed sexual intercourse: Low-dose clomiphene citrate for women with anovulation (e.g., PCOS)

Referral to a specialist is warranted if: Female age >35 and trying >6 months, Abnormal semen parameters, Tubal pathology, endometriosis, or significant menstrual irregularities, No conception despite initial interventions for 6-12 months

question_text: You are taking care of new born babies in a community health center.

sub_questions.text: Describe briefly the components of "Essential neonatal care" recommended by World Health Organization? How will you implement "Essential neonatal care" in your community health center? [5]

components: Immediate and thorough drying - Dry the newborn with a clean, warm towel immediately after birth to prevent hypothermia.
Skin-to-skin contact and thermal protection - Place the baby on the mother's chest (Kangaroo Mother Care - KMC), cover with a warm blanket. Avoid bathing for 24 hours.
Early initiation of exclusive breastfeeding - Start breastfeeding within the first hour of birth. Avoid pre-lacteal feeds.
Clean cord care with delayed cord clamping - Cut cord with sterile blade, keep the cord stump dry and clean, and do not apply harmful substances.

Eye care and immunization - Apply prophylactic antibiotic eye drops or ointment to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum, Administer BCG, OPV-0, and Hepatitis B vaccines as per national immunization schedule.
Rooming in - keep the mother and baby in same room
Vit K injection at birth to prevent bleeding
implementation: Training of staff in neonatal resuscitation, breastfeeding support, infection control.
Ensure availability of supplies - clean towels, sterile cord cutting kits, warm clothing, vaccines.
Create warm environment - prevent draughts, use radiant warmers if needed.
Mother education - promote exclusive breastfeeding, clean cord care, and recognition of danger signs.
Referral system - timely identification and transfer of at-risk newborns to higher centers.
Education of the staff and community

sub_questions.text: How will you provide feeding for the newborn in special situations like twin gestation and pre term infant? [5]

twin_gestation: Encourage breastfeeding both twins - supply generally sufficient with frequent feeding.
Alternate breasts between feeds to ensure equal stimulation.
Provide extra nutritional support to the mother to maintain milk production.

preterm_infant.approach: Direct breastfeeding or expressed breast milk (EBM)
EBM via cup & spoon (32-34) or nasogastric tube (28-31)
IV fluids initially or TPN, then minimal enteral feeding ("trophic feeds") with gradual increase

preterm_infant.Additional notes: Use fortified breast milk or preterm formula if mother's milk is insufficient. Monitor for feeding intolerance, hypoglycemia, and weight gain

question_text: A 5-year-old child is brought to you with complaints of cold, cough and fever since 3 days. Child has poor feeding and lethargy. On examination, the Respiratory rate was 38 per minute.

sub_questions.text: How will you assess a child according to IMNCI for pneumonia? [5]
answer: Check for general danger signs: Inability to drink or breastfeed, Vomits everything, Lethargic or unconscious, Convulsions
Ask about and observe for: Cough or difficult breathing, Duration of symptoms, Any stridor, chest indrawing
Measure respiratory rate (age-specific cut-offs): 2-12 months: ≥50 breaths/min, 1-5 years: ≥40 breaths/min, This child (5 years) with RR 38 → normal respiratory rate
Look for chest indrawing - Lower chest wall indrawing indicates pneumonia
Look and listen for stridor or wheeze - Stridor in a calm child = severe disease, Wheeze may suggest bronchiolitis/asthma

Classify illness based on findings: No pneumonia (cough/cold): RR normal, no indrawing, Pneumonia: Fast breathing or chest indrawing, Severe pneumonia: Any general danger sign or stridor in calm child

sub_questions.text: How will you manage this child? [5]
answer: Classification: This child has RR 38/min (normal for 5 years) but is lethargic and has poor feeding → General danger sign → Classified as Severe Pneumonia or Very Severe Disease
Management steps:
1. Urgent referral to a higher facility for inpatient care
2. While referring, initiate pre-referral treatment:
- First dose of parenteral antibiotic: Inj. Ampicillin (50 mg/kg IM) or Inj. Ceftriaxone (50-80 mg/kg IM/IV)
- Treat fever: Paracetamol if febrile
- Maintain hydration: Start IV fluids if unable to drink
- Humidified Oxygen if signs of hypoxia (SpO₂ <90%, cyanosis, grunting)
3. Explain danger signs to parents and ensure safe and quick referral
4. Monitor vitals and consciousness level during transport
5. Record and communicate findings clearly to the referral center

question_text: A 3-year-old boy, weighing 12 kg, is brought to the OPD with complaints of recurrent loose stools since morning. Child is thirsty and demanding water. Eyes look sunken and skin turgor is lost.

sub_questions.text: How will you assess for dehydration in this child? [5]

assessment_parameters.findings: Drinks eagerly, thirsty (present in this child)
Goes back slowly or very slowly (present in this child)

answer.classification: 2 or more signs (including sunken eyes + drinks eagerly + slow skin pinch) → Some dehydration
answer.note: If child were lethargic, not able to drink, or skin pinch returns very slowly → Severe dehydration

sub_questions.text: According to IMNCI how will you manage the child? [5]
answer: Use Plan B: ORS at the health facility:
1. Give Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS): 75 ml/kg over 4 hours. For this child (12 kg): 75 × 12 = 900 ml ORS over 4 hours
2. Observe and monitor: Give frequent small sips, Watch for vomiting or worsening condition, Reassess after 4 hours
3. Continue breastfeeding or feeding during rehydration
4. After 4 hours: Reassess hydration status, If improved → switch to Plan A (home care with ORS), If not improved or worse → shift to Plan C (IV fluids)

5. Educate caregiver: How to prepare and give ORS at home, Give zinc syrup 20 mg/day for 14 days (10 mg/day if <6 months), Advise when to return (if vomiting, increased stools, fever, or no improvement)

question_text: A 15-year-old boy is brought to you by his mother complaining of poor scholastic performance.

sub_questions.text: What are the problems of adolescence? [5]
answer: Physical changes & body image issues: Puberty-related changes, early/late maturation concerns, acne, obesity.

Mental health problems: Anxiety, depression, poor concentration, learning disabilities, low self-esteem, peer pressure, incomplete sleep / insomnia. Vulnerable to abuse and violence, migration, exploitation. Early marriage and discrimination in girls.
Behavioral problems: Substance abuse (tobacco, alcohol, drugs), aggression, internet addiction, Risk taking behavior, Emotional outburst/anger/irritability, Stress /peer pressure
Nutritional issues: Anemia, undernutrition/malnutrition, eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia), low bone mineral density/ obesity/ increase fast food/oily food

Sexual and reproductive health issues: Lack of knowledge about safe sex, risk of STIs (HIV, gonorrhea, chlamydia), early or unplanned pregnancy, menstrual problems in girls, Rape victim, Increase sexual desires
Lifestyle diseases - asthma, sleep disorder, reflux disease, fatty liver, diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, PCOD.

sub_questions.text: Role of family physician in improving adolescent health in the community. [5]
answer: Early identification and counseling: Detect mental health concerns, learning difficulties, substance abuse, and intervene early.
Health education and awareness: Conduct sessions on nutrition, menstrual hygiene, sexual and reproductive health, substance abuse prevention. Iron folic acid, calcium supplements
Confidential and adolescent-friendly services: Provide a safe, non-judgmental space for adolescents to discuss sensitive issues (confidentiality is key).
Screening and preventive care: Screen for anemia, obesity, vision problems, and immunization (like HPV vaccine). Decrease screen time, Pursue a hobby
Involve family and school: Guide parents to support emotional and academic needs, Collaborate with schools to promote healthy behaviors and identify at-risk adolescents, Positive group

question_text: Eleven year old child staying in a hostel is brought by the warden complaining of behavioral changes with poor scholastic performance which is of recent onset. On exploring further you suspect child sexual abuse.

sub_questions.text: What is POCSO Act? [5]

answer.definition: POCSO Act stands for the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, enacted by the Government of India in 2012.
key_features: Comprehensive protection: Covers all forms of sexual offences against children (<18 years): sexual assault, sexual harassment, pornography, penetrative and non-penetrative sexual abuse.
Gender-neutral law: Applies to both male and female child victims.
Child-friendly procedures: Special procedures for recording evidence, trial in-camera, assistance of support persons/counselors.
Mandatory reporting: Any person (including a doctor or teacher) aware of sexual abuse must report it. Failure to report is punishable.
Timely justice: Designated Special Courts for speedy trial, Strict punishments ranging from 3 years to life imprisonment, depending on the offence
Special Courts: Fast-track courts called Special POCSO Courts ensure quick trials.

Key Amendments (2019 Amendment): Stricter punishments, including death penalty for aggravated penetrative sexual assault. Offences involving child pornography made harsher. Inclusion of online abuse, such as storage or distribution of child sexual materials.
Objectives of the Act: Protect children from sexual offences. Establish child-friendly investigation and trial procedures. Ensure proper medical care and protection for the child.

sub_questions.text: What is the role of family physician in this scenario of suspected child sex abuse? [5]
answer: Recognize warning signs: vigilant to behavioral changes, sudden drop in academics, anxiety, bedwetting, inappropriate sexual behavior or knowledge for age.
Ensure safety and trust: Talk to the child in a calm, supportive, and non-threatening way. Provide a safe space and assure the child they are not at fault.
Mandatory reporting: Inform the Child Welfare Committee or local police immediately as per POCSO Section 19. Reporting is not optional - failure is a punishable offence.

Medical care and documentation: Provide necessary medical treatment, collect forensic evidence (if within 72 hours), and document findings clearly and accurately. Maintain confidentiality except as required by law.
Support and follow-up: Facilitate counseling or psychiatric referral if needed. Provide continuous emotional and psychosocial support to both the child and guardians.
Maintain professional secrecy

question_text: A 32-year-old pregnant lady PRIMI gravida at 37+2 weeks of gestation presents to you with headache and pedal edema. On examination her BP is 160/90mm on two recordings. She has puffy face and her urine albumin is 2+.

sub_questions.text: What is your diagnosis? [1]
sub_questions.answer: Pre-eclampsia - BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions, Proteinuria (≥1+ on dipstick or ≥300 mg/24hr urine), After 20 weeks of gestation, previously normotensive woman. This woman has BP 160/90, pedal edema, puffy face, and 2+ proteinuria at 37+2 weeks

sub_questions.text: How do you evaluate and manage her pregnancy and delivery? [6]

evaluation: Monitor maternal vitals: BP (frequent), pulse, respiratory rate
Urine test: 24-hour urine protein or spot protein/creatinine ratio/ new onset proteinuria
Blood tests: CBC (platelet count)<1 lac, Liver function tests (AST/ALT) > 2 times, Renal function (creatinine, uric acid, electrolytes), Coagulation profile if severe, BSL, homocysteine
Fetal monitoring: Ultrasound: fetal growth, amniotic fluid, Non-stress test (NST) or biophysical profile (BPP), Doppler velocimetry in suspected fetal growth restriction
management: Since the woman is term (≥37 weeks), the preferred option is delivery after stabilization.
Admit the patient for monitoring and management

Control BP if ≥150/100 mmHg: Tab Labetalol 100 mg BD (first-line) or Nifedipine 10 mg orally. IV labetolol for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy: 20mg iv over 10 mins → 20/40mg over 10 mins → 80 mg in 10 mins → max 220mg. IV hydralazine 5-10mg - alternative to labetalol
Seizure prophylaxis if severe pre-eclampsia: Inj. Magnesium sulfate (Pritchard or Zuspan regimen) - iv mgso4 4 g with 10g im in each buttock
Plan for delivery: If maternal and fetal status stable → induction of labour, If complications or cervix unfavorable → cesarean section

sub_questions.text: What are the maternal and fetal complications you anticipate? [3]

maternal_complications: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets)

question_text: A 21-year-old primigravida at 40+5 weeks of gestational age, with no risk factors, had regular antenatal checkup in your primary health centre. She is admitted and induced with misoprostol and was augmented with pitocin this morning.

sub_questions.text: Draw a partogram with the following findings and Discuss the uses of Partogram in monitoring the labour in a Primary Health Centre. [6]

uses_of_partogram: Early detection of abnormal labour (e.g., prolonged/obstructed labour)
Helps decide timely referral to higher centre if labour is not progressing or complications arise.
Monitors fetal well-being via FHR trends.
Assesses uterine contractions and need for augmentation.
Tracks maternal condition: vitals, urine output, temperature.
Promotes effective team communication with real-time graphic summary.

sub_questions.text: When will you repeat the next Per-vaginal examination and What action would you take if cervical dilatation is 7cm and all other parameters are within normal range? [1+3]

answer.next_exam_time: After 2 hours, i.e., at 12 noon, unless any abnormal signs arise (e.g., fetal distress or maternal concerns).
action_if_7cm: Continue monitoring labour - Cervical dilation has progressed by 1 cm in 2 hours → acceptable.
Support active labour: Encourage hydration, emotional support, and ambulation if not contraindicated.
Monitor uterine contractions and FHR closely (half-hourly FHR, 4-hourly vitals, hourly urine).
Do not intervene unnecessarily - as the labour is progressing, allow it to continue naturally.

sub_questions.answer: Acute gastroenteritis with some dehydration - Loose stools, fever, vomiting, sunken eyes, irritability, and active thirst.

answer: Continue normal feeding during and after diarrhoea: Breastfeeding should be continued frequently, Older infants should receive soft, energy-rich foods
Encourage frequent small feeds: Rice porridge, khichdi, mashed banana, curd, and lentils, kanji, dalia
Catch-up feeding post-recovery: Give extra meals (1-2 extra feeds/day) for 2 weeks to regain lost weight
BRAT diet- banana applesauce rice toast- easily digestible food
Probiotics- curd/ buttermilk
Increase fluid intake
Gradual return to normal diet

question_text: Describe the developmental milestones to be attained by a 3 year old child. [4]

sub_questions.text: Describe the developmental milestones to be attained by a 3 year old child. [4]

gross_motor: Walks up stairs with alternate feet
Stands on one foot for a few seconds
fine_motor_self_help: Undresses self, may attempt to dress

sub_questions.text: What are the common causes of delay in developmental milestones of a 3-year-old child, who had reached all his milestones till 18 months of age. [3]

examples: Maternal infections: TORCH (Toxoplasmosis, Others (syphilis), Rubella, CMV, HSV)
Maternal alcohol intake → Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders

sub_questions.text: What are the clinical features of a child with autism? [3]
answer: Impairment in Social Interaction: Poor eye contact, Does not respond to name, Lack of social reciprocity, Poor peer relationship, Blunt facial expressions
Delayed or Atypical Communication: Delayed speech development, Repeats phrases (echolalia), Limited use of gestures, Can't initiate or sustain conversation, Stereotyped or repetitive use of language
Repetitive Behaviors and Restricted Interests: Repetitive movements (hand flapping, rocking), Rigid routines or resistance to change, Intense interest in specific objects or topics
Note: Intelligence is variable, although many children fall in MR by conventional testing but some show isolated remarkable talent

question_text: What are the components of breast milk for a mother of a term baby? Describe the advantages of breast feeding upto the two years of age? Write about baby friendly hospital initiative. [3+4+3]

sub_questions.text: What are the components of breast milk for a mother of a term baby? [3]

nutritional_components: Carbohydrates: Mainly lactose - provides energy and helps gut flora. 6-7gm/day. The galactose is necessary for galactocerebrosides of brain. Lactose help in absorption of calcium.
Proteins: Easily digestible - whey > casein (e.g., lactalbumin, lactoferrin). 0.9-1.1g/dl. Amino acids like laurine & cysteine are necessary for neurological transmission.

Fats: Rich in essential fatty acids and DHA - important for brain development. Rich in PUFA. Also contain omega 2 & 6 which are important for formation of prostaglandins & cholesterol which further is used for steroid hormone formation.
Vitamins and Minerals: Adequate levels for initial months; Vitamin D may need supplementation. Vit A, E, K are present.
immunological_components: Lysozyme, leukocytes, and oligosaccharides - immune protection

sub_questions.text: Describe the advantages of breast feeding up to the two years of age? [4]

for_the_baby: Complete nutrition for first 6 months; continues to complement solids thereafter.
Protection against infections - diarrhea, respiratory illness, otitis media.
Improved cognitive development - higher IQ scores.
Reduced risk of chronic conditions - obesity, type 1 diabetes, allergies.
for_the_mother: Promotes uterine involution (oxytocin effect), reducing postpartum bleeding.
Reduces risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
societal_and_economic_benefits: Reduces healthcare burden from infant illnesses

sub_questions.text: Write about baby friendly hospital initiative. [3]

answer.description: Launched by WHO to promote and support breastfeeding in hospitals.
ten_steps_to_successful_breastfeeding: Have a written breastfeeding policy communicated to all staff.
Train all healthcare staff in skills needed to implement this policy.
Inform pregnant women about the benefits and management of breastfeeding.
Help initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth.
Show mothers how to breastfeed and maintain lactation, even if separated.
Give no food or drink other than breast milk, unless medically indicated.
Rooming-in: Keep mother and baby together 24 hrs/day.
Refer mothers to support groups on discharge.

question_text: A 21-year-old primigravida of 11 week gestation presented to you with history of spotting per vaginum. On examination vitals are stable and cervical os is closed with mild spotting.

sub_questions.text: Define Abortion. [1]
sub_questions.answer: Abortion is the termination of pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation or the expulsion of a fetus weighing less than 500 grams, when it is nonviable outside the uterus.

sub_questions.text: How do you classify abortion? [2]
answer: Threatened abortion - Vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain with closed cervical os, viable pregnancy. Uterine size corresponds to gestational age.
Inevitable abortion - Vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain with open cervix, products not yet expelled (palpable in Cx). Uterine size can be same or smaller. Fetus is often dead.
Incomplete abortion - Partial expulsion of products of conception (POC). Ut. size is smaller than gest. age.
Complete abortion - All POC expelled, uterus empty. no active vaginal bleeding. Ut. size is smaller. Cx. Is closed.
Missed abortion - Fetus is nonviable, retained in uterus with no symptoms. Cervix is closed.
Septic abortion - Abortion complicated by infection.
Recurrent (habitual) abortion - ≥3 consecutive pregnancy losses.

sub_questions.text: What kind of abortion is described in the above patient and how will you manage her? [3]

answer.diagnosis: Threatened Abortion - Symptoms: Spotting, Closed cervical os, Early gestation (11 weeks), Stable vitals
management: Reassure and Advise Rest - No absolute bed rest needed, but reduce physical exertion.
Ultrasound Pelvis (Transvaginal preferred): Assess fetal viability and exclude other causes (e.g., subchorionic hematoma). Rule out for APLA Syndrome.
Supportive Treatment: Folic acid continuation, Progesterone supplementation (if luteal phase defect suspected or threatened abortion confirmed), 100mg daily until 12 wks of gest.
Monitor for progression - If bleeding increases or pain begins, re-evaluate for inevitable or incomplete abortion.

sub_questions.text: Write briefly on medical termination of pregnancy Act. [4]

answer.description: The MTP Act, first enacted in 1971 and amended in 2021, governs legal abortion in India.

details: Social indications - Risk to mother's physical or mental health
Therapeutic - to save the life of mother. Cardiac disease / psychiatric illness/ cervical & breast malignancy.
Eugenic - anencephaly / chromosomal disorder ( Down's ) / genetic ( cystic fibrosis) / teratogenic / radiation exposure / rubella exposure.
Up to 20 weeks: One registered medical practitioner's opinion
20 to 24 weeks: Two medical practitioners' opinion (for special categories: survivors of rape, minors, etc.)
Beyond 24 weeks: Only in case of fetal anomalies after approval by Medical Board
Woman's identity and details are confidential under law
Only registered medical practitioners at approved facilities can perform MTP

One who has got 6 months house surgeon training on obs and gynae.

question_text: a) What is pre-conception counselling? [2] b) What are the goals of preconceptional counselling? [2] c) What are the benefits of preconceptional counselling? [3] d) How do you implement it in your practice? [3]

sub_questions.text: What is pre-conception counselling? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Pre-conception counselling is the medical and educational consultation provided to women (and couples) before conception to optimize health and address risk factors that could affect pregnancy outcome, maternal health, or fetal development. It involves identifying and managing medical, genetic, lifestyle, and environmental factors before pregnancy begins.

sub_questions.text: What are the goals of preconceptional counselling? [2]
answer: Optimize maternal health before conception
Identify and manage risk factors (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, obesity, infections)
Ensure adequate nutrition and supplementation (e.g., folic acid, iron, calcium, vit D and B12)
Educate about healthy behaviors (e.g., avoiding tobacco, alcohol, harmful drugs)
Immunization status assessed and covered completely.

sub_questions.text: What are the benefits of preconceptional counselling? [3]
answer: Reduces the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes - Neural tube defects, low birth weight, preterm delivery, etc.
Improves management of pre-existing medical conditions - E.g., diabetes, epilepsy, thyroid disorders
Promotes healthy behaviors - Smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance, weight management
Early identification of genetic or hereditary risks - Offers carrier screening and genetic counselling
Enhances psychological readiness and informed decision-making

sub_questions.text: How do you implement it in your practice? [3]
answer: Routine Screening during Consultations - Ask reproductive-aged women about pregnancy plans during general or gynecological visits
Medical camps - Provide information on importance of folic acid, healthy diet, vaccinations, and substance avoidance
Allot specific days in ANC OPD - Screen for chronic diseases, infections, and offer referrals to specialists (e.g., endocrinologists, genetic counselors) when needed
Document and Follow-Up - Maintain records and plan regular follow-up visits to ensure continuity of care

sub_questions.text: Describe the mechanisms of action and their side effect profile. [3]

combined_hormonal_contraceptives: Inhibit ovulation by suppressing the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis (↓FSH, ↓LH)
Thicken cervical mucus - prevents sperm penetration
Alter endometrial lining - makes it hostile for implantation, causes hypoplasia
progestin_only_contraceptives: Suppress ovulation (in higher-dose forms like DMPA/implants)

combined_hormonal_contraceptives: Nausea, breast tenderness, headache, weight changes
↑ Risk of thromboembolism, stroke, MI (esp. in smokers >35 years)
May elevate BP, rarely affect liver enzymes
Increases breast and cervical cancer risk
progestin_only_contraceptives: Weight gain, mood changes, decreased libido
Delayed return to fertility (in injectables like DMPA)

sub_questions.text: Write a brief note on emergency contraception. [3]

answer.description: Used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure.
options: Levonorgestrel pill (1.5 mg single dose) - within 72 hours
Ulipristal acetate - progesterone receptor modulator, 30mg to be taken within 120 hours
Yuzpe method - high-dose combined pills. 250 microgram levonogestrol + 50microgram ethinyl estradiol, within 72 hours
Copper IUD - Most effective, within 5 days
mechanism: Increase cervical mucus thickness - inhibits the entry of sperm
Thickens the endometrial lining - conditions unfavourable for implantation
Does not affect implanted pregnancy or cause abortion

question_text: You are running an immunization clinic in your primary health centre. The mothers are very reluctant to come forward for immunization as they are afraid of the Adverse Event Following Immunization.

sub_questions.text: What is the basic concept of Adverse Event Following Immunisation (AEFI)? [2]
sub_questions.answer: An Adverse Event Following Immunization (AEFI) is: Any untoward medical occurrence which follows immunization and does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the vaccine. It includes minor, severe, and serious reactions that can occur due to the vaccine, the injection procedure, or coincidental events. The adverse event may be unfavourable or unintended sign, abnormal lab finding, symptom or disease. It can be either a true event (really a result of vaccine) or coincidental.

sub_questions.text: How do you classify AEFI? [2]
answer: Vaccine reaction - Due to inherent properties of the vaccine (e.g., fever after DPT) e.g. extensive limb swelling following DTP.
Vaccine quality defect related reaction - failure by manufacturer to completely inactivate polio vaccine.
Program error - Due to error in handling, storage, or administration (e.g., abscess due to unsterile injection). E.g. transmission of infection by contaminated multidose vial.
Coincidental event - Unrelated to vaccine (e.g., febrile seizure due to underlying illness)
Unknown/indeterminate - Cause cannot be established
Immunization anxiety related - like vasovagal syncope in an adolescent during vaccination

sub_questions.text: How will you manage AEFI? [2]

minor_aefi: Manage with paracetamol, cold compress, reassurance
Most of them are self limiting
ATT for disseminated BCG infection / osteitis/ osteomyelitis
Incision and drainage for injection site abscess
severe_serious_aefi: Immediate resuscitation: Ensure airway, breathing, circulation
Administer adrenaline for anaphylaxis (0.01 mg/kg IM every 3-5 mins if needed)
Document and report the event as per protocol

sub_questions.text: As a team leader how will you investigate an AEFI? [4]
answer: Notify and report - Inform District Immunization Officer (DIO) and fill AEFI reporting format (Form P) within 24 hours
Establish facts - Verify vaccine batch, expiry date, cold chain maintenance, injection technique, staff involved
Conduct interviews - Speak to affected family, vaccinator, and witnesses to reconstruct the event
Collect and preserve evidence - Vaccine vial, syringe, cold chain records, case sheets. If death occurs, postmortem may be required
Classify and determine causality - Use WHO causality assessment format. Decide if AEFI is vaccine-related, coincidental, or programmatic
Take corrective action - Training for staff, address cold chain or handling lapses, Community communication to maintain public trust

question_text: Mrs Sabina has brought her 5-month-old baby with complaints of mild nasal discharge, otherwise baby is well. So far baby has been on only breast feed. She asks you about initiation of solid food:

sub_questions.text: What is weaning? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Weaning is the gradual process of introducing semi-solid and solid foods to an infant's diet while continuing breastfeeding. It typically starts when breast milk alone is no longer sufficient to meet the baby's nutritional needs. In India it is advised at 6months of age. Started with some semisolid food like banana , cookies, dalia, rice water, daal ka pani. Give small quantities at regular intevals . Before giving any item make sure temperature is neither high nor very low. Ensure heigene of food item and utensil used.

sub_questions.text: Why and when should you wean the babies? [3]
sub_questions.answer: When to start: At 6 months of age (as per WHO and Government of India guidelines) Why weaning is important: Nutritional needs increase (especially for iron, protein, and energy) Supports growth and development Helps develop chewing and swallowing skills

sub_questions.text: How and what type of foods will you advise? [3]
sub_questions.answer: How: Start with one food at a time, small amounts, and soft consistency Gradually increase the variety, quantity, and consistency Maintain hygiene during food preparation What: Start with mashed or pureed foods -- rice, dal, mashed vegetables Gradually introduce fruit pulp, khichdi, suji kheer, mashed potato, banana By 8--9 months -- small lumps, soft finger foods; by 1 year -- family food Avoid salt, sugar, and honey initially.

sub_questions.text: How much complementary feeds should be weaning foods to contribute along with breast milk up to 24 months of age? [2]
sub_questions.answer: As per WHO recommendations: Age Breast milk Complementary food contribution 6--8 months Majority ~200 kcal/day 9--11 months 50% ~300 kcal/day 12--24 months One-third ~550 kcal/day Complementary foods should be adequate in frequency, energy, and nutrient density, and continue breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond.

question_text: A 52-year-old female has not had periods for past 24 months. She comes to you with hot flushes and vaginal dryness:

sub_questions.text: What is menopause and perimenopause? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Menopause is defined as the permanent cessation of menstruation for 12 consecutive months, due to loss of ovarian follicular activity. Average age: ~50 years. Perimenopause refers to the transitional phase before menopause, characterized by irregular periods, and may start several years earlier, often accompanied by menopausal symptoms.

sub_questions.text: What are the various clinical problems a lady goes through during menopause? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Vasomotor symptoms -- Hot flushes, night sweats Urogenital symptoms -- Vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary frequency/infections Psychological symptoms -- Mood swings, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbances Musculoskeletal symptoms -- Joint pain, risk of osteoporosis Sexual dysfunction -- Decreased libido, discomfort during intercourse

sub_questions.text: Write about the management of at least 4 clinical problems during menopause. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Hot flushes/night sweats Lifestyle changes (cool environment, exercise, avoiding caffeine/alcohol) HRT or SSRIs/SNRIs if symptoms are severe Vaginal dryness/dyspareunia Topical estrogen creams, vaginal moisturizers/lubricants Osteoporosis prevention Adequate calcium (1000--1200 mg/day) and vitamin D intake Weight-bearing exercises, bisphosphonates if needed Mood changes and sleep disturbances CBT (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy), relaxation techniques Low-dose antidepressants or HRT in indicated cases

sub_questions.text: What are the benefits and harms of Hormone Replacement Therapy? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Benefits: Effective relief of vasomotor symptoms Improves vaginal atrophy and urogenital symptoms Helps maintain bone density, reducing fracture risk May improve mood and sleep Harms: Increased risk of thromboembolism Breast cancer risk with prolonged use of combined estrogen-progestin Endometrial hyperplasia if unopposed estrogen is used in women with uterus Stroke risk (especially in older women)

sub_questions.text: What is the grade of PEM as per IAP? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Indian Academy of Pediatrics (IAP) Classification of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM): PEM grading is done based on weight for age (compared to expected weight): Expected weight at 11 months ≈ 8.8--9 kg (average is 3 × birth weight at 1 year) Actual weight = 6.3 kg % of expected ≈70% → This is Grade II PEM as per IAP classification: Grade Weight for age (%) I 71--80% II 61--70% III 51--60% IV <50%

sub_questions.text: What are the common social factors that might have contributed? [3]

Less food consumption by women of the house , ultimately affecting the child Discrimnation against female child. Illitracy -- no education to mother and family about importance of nutrition.

sub_questions.text: What are the indications of admission for a patient with PEM? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Severe acute malnutrition with complications: Weight-for-height < -3 SD, or visible severe wasting Edema, lethargy, or anorexia Associated infections or complications: Persistent diarrhea, pneumonia, or high fever Failure to thrive despite outpatient treatment Inability to feed orally

sub_questions.text: What food regime in the initial phase would you advise and how will be the increase in calorie and protein intake? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Initial phase (Stabilization Phase - Days 1--7): Use F-75 diet: Provides 75 kcal and 0.9--1 g protein per 100 ml Given frequently (8--12 feeds/day) Helps in metabolic stabilization without overloading Transition Phase (Day 7--10): Switch to F-100 diet gradually: 100 kcal and 2.9 g protein per 100 ml Rehabilitation Phase (After day 10): Increase calorie intake to 150--220 kcal/kg/day Protein to 4--6 g/kg/day Introduce energy-dense family foods and continue breastfeeding

question_text: A 32-year-old female, P2L2 sterilized, has presented to you with history of heavy menstrual bleed (HMBL) for past 5 days. Her earlier periods were regular and lasted for 3 days. She had similar episode in last cycle, but since she noticed relatively excess bleeding this month, she came to consult you.

sub_questions.text: What is Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB)? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) refers to bleeding from the uterus that is irregular in volume, duration, or frequency and not related to pregnancy. In reproductive-age women, it may present as heavy, prolonged, frequent, or intermenstrual bleeding. The term replaces older terms like "menorrhagia" or "metrorrhagia." The abnormality can be during the time of actual menses or in between cycle. The quantity og bleeding can more or less than normal It can be with pain or without pain. It can occur at any age from teenage to postmenopause.

sub_questions.text: What is the etiology of AUB according to FIGO Classification? [3]
sub_questions.answer: The FIGO classification system for AUB uses the acronym PALM-COEIN: Structural causes (PALM) Non-structural causes (COEIN) P -- Polyp C -- Coagulopathy A -- Adenomyosis O -- Ovulatory dysfunction L -- Leiomyoma E -- Endometrial M -- Malignancy/Hyperplasia I -- Iatrogenic N -- Not yet classified

sub_questions.text: How will you manage AUB in adolescents, perimenopausal, nonpregnant reproductive age group, and in post-menopausal women? [5]
sub_questions.answer: Adolescents: Often due to immature HPO axis or bleeding disorders Treatment: NSAIDs (e.g. mefenamic acid) Tranexamic acid Low-dose combined oral contraceptives (COCs) Iron supplementation if anemic Evaluate for bleeding disorders (e.g. vWD) Reproductive-age women (non-pregnant): Rule out pregnancy-related causes first Investigate with pelvic exam, ultrasound, CBC, TSH Treatment depends on cause: Hormonal therapy: COCs, progestins NSAIDs, tranexamic acid Endometrial ablation or hysterectomy for resistant cases Myomectomy for fibroids if indicated Perimenopausal women: AUB often due to anovulatory cycles, polyps, or fibroids Must rule out malignancy: Pap smear, TVUS, endometrial biopsy Treatment: Hormonal therapy (e.g. cyclic progesterone or LNG-IUS) Surgical: Hysteroscopy for polyps, ablation, or hysterectomy if indicated Postmenopausal women: ALWAYS evaluate thoroughly due to high risk of endometrial carcinoma Investigations: TVUS (endometrial thickness), endometrial biopsy Management depends on cause: Polyps or malignancy → surgical removal Hormone therapy (only after malignancy is ruled out)

sub_questions.text: What are the various types of discharge you see on vaginal examination? [3]

sub_questions.text: How will you manage this patient? [2]

sub_questions.text: Write briefly on the management of sexually transmitted infections. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Syndromic approach (recommended in primary care): History and examination to identify syndromes: Vaginal discharge Urethral discharge Genital ulcer Lower abdominal pain Inguinal swelling Treatment based on syndrome, using WHO/NACO guidelines: Dual therapy for gonorrhea/chlamydia: *Azithromycin + Cefixime/Ceftriaxone* Metronidazole for trichomoniasis/bacterial vaginosis Acyclovir for herpes Benzathine penicillin for syphilis Partner notification and treatment Counselling: Safe sex practices Condom promotion Follow-up and referral if no improvement or complications Health education and IEC activities in the community

question_text: A five-day-old neonate is brought to you with history of poor feeding and yellowish discolouration of skin over the past two days.

sub_questions.text: Describe the differential diagnoses and the pathophysiology of neonatal jaundice. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Differential Diagnoses: Physiological jaundice (most common): Appears after 24 hours, peaks at day 3--5, resolves within a week in term infants. Breastfeeding jaundice: Due to insufficient intake, leads to dehydration and increased enterohepatic circulation. Breast milk jaundice: Due to substances in breast milk that inhibit conjugation. Severe prematurity Hemolytic disease (e.g. Rh or ABO incompatibility): Causes early and severe jaundice. Hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia and G6PD deficiency polycythemia Sepsis: May present with jaundice along with poor feeding, fever, or lethargy. Delayed cord clamping Cephalhematoma Congenital hypothyroidism or biliary atresia: Causes prolonged jaundice. Crigler najjar syndrome, gilbert syndrome, down syn. Obstructive causes- congenital hepatic fibrosis, caroli's ds, extra hepatic biliary atresia, choledochal cyst , stone or stricture Pathophysiology: Neonates have: Increased red blood cell mass (higher bilirubin load). Shorter RBC lifespan (90 days). Immature liver enzymes (↓UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity). Increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. Unconjugated bilirubin, if high, may cross the blood-brain barrier and lead to kernicterus.

sub_questions.text: Describe the risk factors for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. [2]
sub_questions.answer: Prematurity (<37 weeks) ABO or Rh incompatibility G6PD deficiency or other hemolytic conditions Cephalohematoma or bruising Delayed cord clamp Exclusive breastfeeding with poor intake Sibling with history of neonatal jaundice

sub_questions.text: How would you assess the severity of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Clinical assessment using Kramer's rule: Jaundice progresses from head to toe (5 zones). Approximate bilirubin levels based on the area involved. Serum bilirubin estimation: Total Serum Bilirubin (TSB) -- most reliable. Transcutaneous bilirubinometer -- for screening. Severity is based on TSB levels adjusted for postnatal age (hours) and gestational age using nomograms.

sub_questions.text: Describe the indications and treatment options for neonatal jaundice. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Indications for treatment: TSB above phototherapy threshold (based on age in hours and risk category). >15mg/dl in 24-48hrs of age ; >18mg/dl in 48-72 hrs ; >20mg/dl in >72hrs of age Rapid rise in bilirubin (>0.2 mg/dL/hour). Jaundice within first 24 hours. Any signs of bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, hypotonia). TSB approaching exchange transfusion level. Treatment Options: Phototherapy (mainstay): Converts bilirubin to water-soluble forms (lumirubin) excreted without conjugation. MOA- photo isomerization ; structural isomerization ; photo oxidation Exchange transfusion: In cases of severe hyperbilirubinemia or failure of phototherapy. Treat underlying cause: Antibiotics for sepsis. IV fluids for dehydration. Stop hemolysis (e.g., in Rh incompatibility).

sub_questions.text: What is postpartum haemorrhage and how do you classify? [3]
sub_questions.answer: PPH is blood loss ≥500 mL after vaginal delivery or ≥1000 mL after cesarean within 24 hours of delivery (primary PPH) or after 24 hours to 6 weeks (secondary PPH). Clinically PPH is any amount of bleeding from or intogenital travt following birth of baby up the end of puerperium , which adversely affects the general condition of patient evidenced by rise in pulse rate anf falling blood pressure . Classification: Primary (Early) PPH: Occurs within 24 hours of delivery. a ) third stage hmg b) true postpartum hmg Secondary (Late) PPH: Occurs after 24 hours up to 6 weeks postpartum.

sub_questions.text: What are the risk factors of PPH? [2]

sub_questions.text: How will you manage her? [3]

Resuscitate: IV fluids (normal saline or Ringer's lactate) Send clood for CBC , cross matching , prepare for blood transfusion. Monitor vitals, urine output, and blood loss. Keep pt flat & warm Give oxygen Evaluate and Manage Cause (4 Ts): Tone (Uterine atony -- most common) Fundal massage Uterotonics: oxytocin infusion, methylergometrine (if not hypertensive), misoprostol Tissue (Retained products) Manual exploration or uterine curettage if retained placenta suspected Trauma (Cervical/vaginal tear, uterine rupture) Inspect and repair lacerations Thrombin (Coagulopathy) Check coagulation profile and treat accordingly If bleeding persists: Use uterine tamponade (e.g., Bakri balloon / condom catheter / sengstaken blackemore tube/ foley's catheter . Uterine packing with 5metre long gauze Consider surgical options: uterine artery ligation, ovarian A. ligation , ant. division of internal iliac A., B-Lynch suture, hysterectomy if unresponsive

question_text: A 43-year-old lady presented with complaints of post coital bleeding and intermenstrual bleeding since last 4 weeks:

sub_questions.text: What is the aetiology/risk factors, clinical features of carcinoma cervix? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Risk factors - Persistent infection with high-risk HPV (especially types 16 and 18) -- most important risk factor Early onset of sexual activity Multiple sexual partners Immunosuppression (e.g., HIV) Smoking Low socioeconomic status Poor genital hygiene Long-term use of oral contraceptives (>5 years) High parity Clinical features- Intermenstrual bleeding Post coital bleeding Foul-smelling vaginal discharge Pelvic pain or dyspareunia Advanced disease: weight loss, leg swelling, backache, haematuria, or rectal symptoms

sub_questions.text: Which are the methods of screening for cervical cancer? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Pap smear (Papanicolaou test): Cytological screening; done every 3 years (age 21--65) HPV DNA testing: Detects high-risk HPV; done every 5 years (alone or with Pap smear). Started after 30yrs of age. Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA): acetic acid coagulates proyeins, which appear opaque and white s/o premalignant or cancerous changes. Visual inspection with lugol's iodine application -- abnormal cells lacks glycogen, remain unstained , appear yellow Liquid based monolayers Automated cytologival screening Colposcopy Cervicography Vedio colpography Speculoscopy

sub_questions.text: How do you diagnose and manage cervical intraepithelial neoplasia? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Diagnosis: Colposcopy-guided biopsy -- after abnormal Pap/HPV test Histopathology -- confirms CIN grade (CIN 1, 2, or 3) Management: CIN 1 (mild dysplasia): Observation with repeat cytology/HPV testing in 6--12 months CIN 2 or 3 (moderate to severe dysplasia): Ablative methods: Cryotherapy, laser ablation (if no invasion suspected) Excisional methods: LEEP (Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure), cold knife conization Follow-up with repeat Pap/HPV test and colposcopy as per guidelines

question_text: A lady who underwent Caesarean section recently comes to you with her husband for temporary contraception advice.

sub_questions.text: List all the temporary methods of contraception that this couple can use. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Barrier methods: Male condoms Female condoms Diaphragms Vaginal sponge Hormonal methods: Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) -- not immediately post-CS Progestin-only pills (POPs) -- safe postpartum Injectable contraceptives (e.g., DMPA , NET-EN , combination) Implants (e.g., Nexplanon / norplant- II / LNG rod) Transdermal patch Devices : Copper-T (Cu-T) -- can be inserted after 6 weeks postpartum LNG-IUS (Levonorgestrel Intrauterine System) Vaginal rings Transcervical ( ESSURE) Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM): If criteria are met (exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhea, <6 months postpartum) Fertility Awareness Methods: Calendar method, basal body temperature, cervical mucus method

sub_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages. [3+2]
sub_questions.answer: Method Advantages Disadvantages Barrier (Condoms) No systemic side effects, May reduce sexual pleasure, prevents STIs, easily user-dependent accessible Oral Pills Reversible, regularizes Requires daily intake, COCPs (COCPs/POPs) cycles, some protection contraindicated in against ovarian & breastfeeding or immediate endometrial cancers postpartum Injectables Long-acting (every 3 Irregular bleeding, delay in months), effective, safe return to fertility, weight during breastfeeding gain Implants 3--5 years protection, Needs minor procedure for highly effective, safe for insertion/removal, menstrual lactating women irregularities IUD Long-term (5--10 years), Risk of expulsion, (Copper-T/LNG-IUS) reversible, safe for pain/cramping, spotting, breastfeeding women needs trained provider LAM Natural, no cost, provides Effective only under strict nutrition and bonding criteria (<6 months, exclusive BF, amenorrhea)

sub_questions.text: What is your advice for the couple? [2]
sub_questions.answer: If the mother is exclusively breastfeeding and amenorrheic (baby <6 months): She can rely on Lactational Amenorrhea Method temporarily. Postpartum (6 weeks and above or not meeting LAM criteria): Progestin-only methods (POPs, DMPA injections, implants) are safe and effective. IUD (Copper-T or LNG-IUS) can be inserted after 6 weeks. Barrier method (condoms) can be used anytime and is also protective against STIs. Counsel on dual protection (e.g., condoms + POPs) and plan for long-term method later if appropriate.

question_text: Mr. B, an HIV positive patient, with supressed viral load gets married. The wife knows his condition and the couple is practising safe sex. Mr. B gives a frantic call saying that the condom ruptured during intercourse.

sub_questions.text: What advice will you provide to the couple? [5]
sub_questions.answer: This is a serodiscordant couple (one partner HIV-positive, the other negative). Not to panic -- Mr. B has a suppressed viral load, meaning "Undetectable = Untransmittable" So the risk of HIV transmission is extremely low. Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for the wife: If she's not on pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), start PEP within 72 hours of the exposure. Duration: 28 days. PEP regimen typically includes: Tenofovir + Emtricitabine (Truvada) + Dolutegravir or Raltegravir HIV testing: Baseline HIV test now. Repeat at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months post-exposure to confirm serostatus. Continue PrEP after PEP (optional): Especially if the couple plans to remain sexually active without consistent condom use. Counseling and reassurance: Emphasize continued ART adherence for Mr. B. Reinforce open communication, emotional support, and safe sex education.

sub_questions.text: After 2 years of marriage, they decide to conceive a child. What advice and precautions will you give? [5]
sub_questions.answer: Pre-Conception Counseling: Ensure Mr. B maintains an undetectable viral load (test within past 6 months). Screen for other STIs in both partners and treat if needed. Assess wife's HIV status -- must be negative and on PrEP if conception is planned. Timed unprotected intercourse: Allow condomless sex only during fertile window (ovulation period) to reduce exposure frequency. Continue ART for Mr. B and start PrEP for the wife prior to attempts at conception. Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) for the wife: Start Tenofovir + Emtricitabine (Truvada) daily before conception attempts and continue until at least 4--6 weeks after. Alternatives to natural conception (optional, if resources available): Sperm washing + Intrauterine Insemination (IUI) or IVF -- especially if Mr. B's viral suppression is uncertain or couple prefers zero risk. During pregnancy: Continue regular HIV testing for the wife. Monitor Mr. B's ART adherence and viral load.

question_text: A 54-year-old post menopausal lady comes with history of white discharge per vagina (WDPV).

sub_questions.text: What is the differential diagnosis? [4]
sub_questions.answer: In a postmenopausal woman, WDPV warrants suspicion of benign, infective, or malignant causes. D/D's Atrophic vaginitis (most common): Due to estrogen deficiency Dryness, irritation, thin discharge Vaginal or cervical infections: Candidiasis (rare in postmenopause unless diabetic or immunocompromised) Bacterial vaginosis Trichomoniasis (less common postmenopause) Cervical polyp or erosion Genital malignancy: Carcinoma cervix Carcinoma endometrium Carcinoma vagina (Malignancy must always be ruled out in postmenopausal discharge, especially if foul-smelling or blood-tinged)

sub_questions.text: What investigations will help you to decide the cause of WDPV? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Speculum and per speculum examination: Inspect for growth, bleeding, polyps, vaginal atrophy High Vaginal Swab (HVS): For wet mount, Gram stain, KOH mount to rule out infections Pap smear (cervical cytology): To screen for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or cancer Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal): Evaluate endometrial thickness, masses, or polyps Endometrial biopsy (if indicated): Especially if thickened endometrium or spotting is present

sub_questions.text: How can this be managed in a community health centre? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Initial assessment and basic treatment: Treat presumed infections empirically (e.g., antifungal, metronidazole) Topical estrogen cream for atrophic vaginitis (if available and diagnosis confirmed) Counseling and hygiene education: Emphasize perineal hygiene, avoid douching, cotton underwear Pap smear collection and swab tests Send to higher centre if facility not available on-site Refer to higher if CIN --II/III

sub_questions.text: What are the indications for referral? [1]
sub_questions.answer: Suspicion of malignancy (e.g., blood-stained discharge, cervical growth) Persistent or recurrent discharge despite treatment Abnormal Pap smear or thickened endometrium Lack of diagnostic or therapeutic facilities at PHC

question_text: A 60-year-old lady comes with a mass that protrudes from the vagina when she voids. She is also upset that she sometimes "leaks urine".

sub_questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis? [1]
sub_questions.answer: Most likely diagnosis: Uterovaginal prolapse with stress urinary incontinence

sub_questions.text: Discuss the clinical examinaion to assess her. [2]
sub_questions.answer: General and pelvic examination: Inspect for prolapse of uterus, vaginal walls (cystocele, rectocele) during straining or coughing Note the degree of prolapse (use POP-Q or traditional grading) Speculum and bimanual exam: Assess vaginal wall integrity, cervix, and uterine position Rule out other pelvic pathology Incontinence assessment: Cough stress test: observe for leakage on coughing Check residual urine if retention is suspected Pad test Q- tip test

sub_questions.text: How will you manage her in the family practice setting? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Education and reassurance: Explain the benign nature of prolapse and urinary leakage Lifestyle modifications (e.g., avoid heavy lifting, manage chronic cough/constipation) Pelvic floor exercises: Kegel exercises to strengthen pelvic muscles Regularly supervised training may improve outcomes Pessary fitting: Vaginal pessary device as a temporary or long-term non-surgical measure Medical management: Topical estrogen cream (if atrophic changes present) Treat urinary tract infection if present

sub_questions.text: When will you refer the patient for surgery and how will you prepare the patient for surgery? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Refer for surgery if: Symptomatic stage II or higher prolapse not relieved by conservative measures Recurrent urinary incontinence or urinary retention Recurrent UTIs or ulceration of prolapsed tissue Patient's preference after understanding non-surgical options Pre-surgical preparation: Optimize medical conditions (e.g., diabetes, hypertension) Screening: Pap smear, pelvic ultrasound, urine analysis Counselling about procedure, risks, postoperative care, and sexual function Fitness for anesthesia: Pre-anesthetic check-up and basic labs

question_text: A 7-year-old child has been advised to undergo dental extraction. The patient has Tetralogy of Fallot. What advice will you give the parents and the dentist? [10]

sub_questions.text: What advice will you give the parents and the dentist? [10]
sub_questions.answer: Endocarditis Prophylaxis Child is high-risk for infective endocarditis. Give antibiotic prophylaxis 30--60 minutes before procedure: Amoxicillin: 50 mg/kg orally (max 2g) If allergic: Clindamycin 20 mg/kg orally Choose a dental setting with medical support Extraction should be done in a hospital-based dental unit or setup with pediatric and cardiac emergency support. Preoperative Assessment Dental team must consult the pediatric cardiologist before procedure. Evaluate: Baseline oxygen saturation Cyanotic spell history Current cardiac medications (e.g., propranolol) Hematocrit (polycythemia is common) Positioning and Oxygenation Keep child in a semi-upright position Ensure oxygen supply is available and ready for use Avoid triggers for cyanotic spells Avoid stress, dehydration, pain, and hypoxia Use pain control (topical + local anesthetic) Avoid excessive crying or struggling -- consider sedation if needed Local anesthesia precautions Use vasoconstrictor-free local anesthetics or minimal epinephrine (High doses of epinephrine can worsen right-to-left shunt and hypoxia) Postoperative care Maintain hydration and oxygenation Continue oral antibiotics if advised by cardiologist Monitor for signs of infection, fever, or breathlessness

question_text: A 4-year-old-girl is brought to you by her parents as she has been crying continuously and rubbing her left ear.

sub_questions.text: What are the likely causes? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Causes of Ear Pain Acute Otitis Media (AOM) -- Most common; infection behind the eardrum. Otitis Externa -- Infection of the outer ear canal ("swimmer's ear"). Foreign body in ear canal -- Common in children. Impacted cerumen (earwax) Referred pain -- From throat infection, dental caries, or tonsillitis. Trauma -- From inserting objects in ear.

sub_questions.text: What physical signs will be seen in different conditions and how will you manage each one of them? [4+4]
sub_questions.answer: Condition Physical Signs Management 1. Acute Otitis Media - Red, bulging tympanic membrane - Paracetamol for pain and fever - Loss of light reflex - Amoxicillin 40--50 mg/kg/day × 5--7 days if bacterial - Tender mastoid - Nasal saline if URI present 2. Otitis Externa - Pain on pinna/tragus movement - Clean ear canal - Swollen, red external canal - Topical antibiotic + steroid drops (e.g., ciprofloxacin + - Discharge dexamethasone) - Analgesics 3. Foreign Body - Visible object in ear canal - Do not irrigate if object is organic - Irritation, discharge, foul smell - Refer for ENT removal (if organic) - Analgesics if needed 4. Impacted Wax - Wax visible on otoscopy - Wax softeners (glycerin, hydrogen peroxide drops) - Dull hearing or pain - Syringing if soft - TM not visualized - Avoid self-cleaning by parents 5. question_text: An 8-year-old girl comes with history of passing high coloured urine and headache. 3 weeks ago she was treated for scabies.

sub_questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (APSGN) A classic presentation after skin infection (impetigo/scabies) or pharyngitis due to Group A Streptococcus. Key symptoms: cola-colored urine (hematuria), headache (from hypertension), ± facial puffiness.

sub_questions.text: What laboratory tests will confirm the diagnosis? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Urinalysis Hematuria (RBCs), proteinuria, RBC casts Serum Complement C3 Typically low in APSGN Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titre or Anti-DNase B titre Elevated, indicating recent streptococcal infection Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) and Serum Creatinine To assess renal function Blood pressure and urine output monitoring Chest x ray -- vascular markings visible

sub_questions.text: What treatment can be given to manage her in a communtity health centre? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Bed Rest -- During acute phase to reduce workload on kidneys Antihypertensives (if BP > 95th percentile for age) Example: Nifedipine or Amlodipine Avoid ACE inhibitors ( risk of hyperkalemia) Salt and Fluid Restriction -- If edema or hypertension is present Furosemide -- For managing edema and hypertension. p/o 1-3mg/kg till edemadisappear; i/v 2-4mg/kg if pulmonary edema Monitor weight, urine output, and BP daily Antibiotics -- Only if active skin infection persists (e.g., Amoxicillin) Hemodialysis if heart failure / prolonged oliguria

sub_questions.text: When should the child be referred to a major centre? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Refer if the child has: Severe hypertension not controlled with initial therapy Oliguria or anuria (urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hour) Rising serum creatinine or urea Seizures, encephalopathy, or signs of fluid overload (e.g., pulmonary edema) Persistent proteinuria/hematuria beyond 6--8 weeks

question_text: A 2nd standard student is brought by his mother to the hospital with fever and running nose for the past 5 days. He has received all his immunisations from the local PHC. He has a vescicular rash all over the body for the past 2 days which first started on his chest and spread out .

sub_questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Most likely diagnosis Chickenpox (Varicella) Caused by Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) Classical progression of rash: Macules → Papules → Vesicles → Pustules → Crusting, beginning on the trunk and spreading outward (centrifugal distribution) Associated with fever, coryza, and malaise

sub_questions.text: How will you manage this patient? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Symptomatic treatment Antipyretics: Paracetamol for fever (Avoid aspirin → risk of Reye's syndrome) Antihistamines: For itching (e.g., Chlorpheniramine) Topical calamine lotion: For skin soothing General care Keep skin clean and dry Trim nails to prevent secondary bacterial infection Ensure adequate hydration and rest Antiviral therapy (only in special cases): Not routinely indicated in healthy children May be considered if child is immunocompromised or has severe disease (Acyclovir if started within 24--48 hours of rash onset)

sub_questions.text: How will you prevent the infection from spreading in the community as well as in the family? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Isolation of patient Keep the child at home until all vesicles crust over (usually 5--7 days after rash appears) Avoid school and public contact Hygiene practices Hand hygiene for all family members Avoid sharing personal items like towels, clothing, toys Vaccination Varicella vaccine: Should be given to all unvaccinated children >12 months and susceptible adults May be offered as post-exposure prophylaxis within 3--5 days for close contacts Protect vulnerable contacts Keep the infected child away from pregnant women, immunocompromised persons, and newborns If such contacts are exposed, consult physician for Varicella-Zoster Immune Globulin (VZIG) or antiviral prophylaxis

question_text: A 3-year-old boy had high grade fever and developed generalised seizures. He recovered rapidly and is otherwise well now.

sub_questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis? What are the clinical features of this condition? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Most likely diagnosis: Febrile Seizure ( simple type) Clinical Features: Occurs between 6 months and 5 years of age Associated with fever >38°C (100.4°F) Generalised tonic-clonic seizure Lasts <15 minutes No recurrence within 24 hours No signs of CNS infection (e.g., meningitis) or prior afebrile seizures Normal development before and after seizure

sub_questions.text: What treatment will you administer? [1]
sub_questions.answer: No specific treatment is required after a simple febrile seizure if the child is stable If seizure is ongoing: IV/rectal benzodiazepine (e.g., Diazepam, Midazolam) Treat underlying cause of fever (e.g., paracetamol for viral illness) Reassurance and observation

sub_questions.text: What is the controversy in the treatment of this condition? [1]
sub_questions.answer: Controversy: Whether to use anticonvulsants prophylactically (e.g., phenobarbital, valproate) to prevent recurrence Current consensus: Routine prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended due to potential side effects outweighing benefits for simple febrile seizures

sub_questions.text: What advice will you provide the parents for prevention of this conditon? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Monitor and manage fever early Use paracetamol/ibuprofen at onset of fever Tepid sponging if fever persists Ensure hydration and rest during febrile illnesses Educate about seizure first aid Place child on side Protect from injury Do not put anything in the mouth Seek medical help if seizure >5 minutes or recurrence

sub_questions.answer: Prognosis is excellent in simple febrile seizures Most children do not develop epilepsy (risk <2--3%) Normal intelligence and development expected About 1/3 may have recurrence of febrile seizures, especially if: First seizure before 18 months Family history of febrile seizures Fever not very high at onset of seizure

question_text: Baby born 17 hours ago, was found to be icteric on examination. Baby is feeding well:

sub_questions.text: Explain the bilirubin metabolism. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Bilirubin Metabolism Production: Bilirubin is primarily produced from the breakdown of heme in hemoglobin. Senescent red blood cells are destroyed in the reticuloendothelial system, producing unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. Transport: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and transported in the blood bound to albumin to the liver. Conjugation: In hepatocytes, UDP-glucuronyl transferase converts unconjugated bilirubin into conjugated (direct) bilirubin, which is water-soluble. Excretion: Conjugated bilirubin is excreted into bile, enters the intestine, and is eliminated in feces. Some is converted into urobilinogen and excreted in urine.

sub_questions.text: How will you manage this baby? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Management (Icteric at 17 hours of life) Since jaundice appears within 24 hours, this is always pathological and needs urgent evaluation. Assess clinical status: Check for activity, tone, feeding, vitals, and signs of encephalopathy. Investigations: Total and direct serum bilirubin levels Blood group and Coombs test (for ABO/Rh incompatibility) Hemoglobin, hematocrit, reticulocyte count (for hemolysis) CBC, peripheral smear (for infection/hemolysis) CRP, blood culture (if sepsis suspected) HPLC, G6PD Initiate Phototherapy: Based on bilirubin level and age in hours, start phototherapy per AAP nomogram. Ensure adequate hydration and feeding. Cover eyes & genetelia Repeat bilirubin levels every 6--12 hours depending on trend and severity. If bilirubin reaches exchange transfusion threshold or shows signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, refer to NICU for exchange transfusion.

question_text: Mrs. Rajani, primigravida, 38 weeks of gestation, admitted in the labor room of secondary care setting. She was induced for high blood pressure. Her BP at admission was recorded to be 164/112, Urine Albumin ++:

sub_questions.text: Define preeclampsia and severe preeclampsia. [4]
sub_questions.answer: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder that occurs after 20 weeks of gestation, characterized by: Blood Pressure ≥140/90 mmHg measured on two occasions at least 4 hours apart AND Proteinuria: ≥300 mg in 24-hour urine collection, or ≥1+ on dipstick test, or Protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3 Severe Preeclampsia is defined when any one of the following features are present: Severe hypertension: BP ≥160/110 mmHg on two occasions, 4 hours apart Heavy proteinuria (≥3+ or >5 g/day) Neurological symptoms: severe headache, visual disturbances Epigastric/RUQ pain Elevated liver enzymes, low platelets Renal impairment or oliguria Pulmonary edema Fetal growth restriction (IUGR)

sub_questions.text: Discuss the management of this patient. [6]
sub_questions.answer: Management of This Patient (Severe Preeclampsia at 38 Weeks) Admission and Monitoring Admit Monitor: BP every 15--30 min until stabilized Pulse, respiratory rate Urine output (catheterize, target >30 ml/hour) Fetal well-being (CTG) Control Blood Pressure Start antihypertensives: Labetalol IV: 20 mg bolus, may repeat at 10-minute intervals f/b 40 -80 (max 300 mg) OR Hydralazine IV: 5--10 mg slowly every 20--30 mins OR Nifedipine oral: 10 mg (immediate release), repeat in 30 mins if needed Target BP: 140--150 / 90--100 mmHg Prevent Eclampsia (Seizures) Magnesium Sulfate therapy: Loading dose: 4 g IV over 15--20 min IM dose: 10 g IM (5 g each buttock) OR IV infusion (1 g/hr) Maintenance: 5 g IM every 4 hrs OR IV infusion for 24 hrs after delivery Monitor for toxicity (patellar reflex, RR >12/min, urine output >30 ml/hr) Antidote for toxicity: Calcium gluconate 10 ml IV slowly Plan for Delivery At 38 weeks with severe preeclampsia, delivery is the definitive treatment As she has already been induced, allow vaginal delivery if: Maternal and fetal status is stable No obstetric contraindication Consider cesarean section if: Labour doesn't progress Fetal distress Worsening maternal condition Postpartum Care Continue Magnesium Sulfate for 24 hours after delivery Monitor BP, urine output, and signs of eclampsia Continue antihypertensives if needed (labetalol, nifedipine safe postpartum)
