question_text: Pregnancy is one of the risk factors for UTI:

sub_questions.text: Explain why a pregnant lady is at risk for UTI. [4]
sub_questions.answer: Pregnancy increases the risk of urinary tract infections (UTI) due to anatomical, hormonal, and physiological changes: Progesterone effect: Relaxation of smooth muscles leads to ureteral dilatation (hydroureter), urinary stasis. Decreased ureteric peristalsis delays urine flow, promoting bacterial growth. Mechanical compression: Enlarging uterus compresses ureters and bladder neck, leading to urinary stasis and incomplete bladder emptying. Glycosuria and aminoaciduria: Pregnancy-associated changes in renal handling increase excretion of glucose and amino acids, providing a nutrient-rich medium for bacterial growth. Decreased immune response: Relative immunosuppression during pregnancy makes it easier for pathogens like E. coli to colonize and ascend. Increased bladder volume and decreased tone: Leads to incomplete emptying, contributing to urinary retention and infection risk.

sub_questions.text: How would you manage a pregnant lady with UTI at various stages of pregnancy? [6]
sub_questions.answer: General Principles at All Stages: Urine culture and sensitivity: confirm diagnosis and guide antibiotics. Start empirical antibiotics (after sending culture) -- later adjust based on sensitivity. Hydration: Encourage oral fluids. Follow-up: Repeat urine culture after treatment. Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (any trimester): Common in pregnancy and must be treated to prevent pyelonephritis. Antibiotics for 5--7 days: Nitrofurantoin (avoid in 1st trimester and after 37 weeks) Cephalexin Amoxicillin-clavulanate Symptomatic Lower UTI (Cystitis): Symptoms: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain. Antibiotics same as above for 7 days. Monitor for signs of ascending infection (fever, flank pain). Educate about personal hygiene and voiding habits. Upper UTI (Pyelonephritis): Symptoms: Fever, flank pain, vomiting, chills. Needs hospitalization, IV fluids, and IV antibiotics: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime Switch to oral antibiotics after 48--72 hours of improvement. Total duration: 10--14 days. Monitor maternal and fetal well-being (risk of preterm labor, sepsis). Recurrence / Persistent UTI: Repeat culture and sensitivity. Consider low-dose prophylactic antibiotics for remainder of pregnancy if recurrent (e.g., nitrofurantoin 50--100 mg at bedtime). Rule out structural abnormalities.

sub_questions.text: How will you manage Abnormal uterine bleed (Investigation and treatment)? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Investigations: CBC -- for anemia Thyroid profile -- TSH Pelvic ultrasound -- uterus and adnexa Endometrial sampling/biopsy -- if > 40 years, or high risk for endometrial hyperplasia Pap smear -- to rule out cervical pathology Coagulation profile -- if history suggests coagulopathy Treatment: Medical Management For Acute Severe Bleeding High-dose IV estrogen (conjugated equine estrogen) High-dose combined oral contraceptives (COCs) High-dose progestins (e.g., medroxyprogesterone acetate) Tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic) NSAIDs (e.g., mefenamic acid) For Chronic AUB Hormonal therapy: COCs -- regulate cycles, reduce flow. Progestins (cyclical or continuous). Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) -- very effective in reducing menstrual blood loss. GnRH agonists (temporary use, especially for fibroids/adenomyosis). Non-hormonal therapy: Tranexamic acid (during menses). NSAIDs (reduce prostaglandin-mediated bleeding). Surgical Management (if medical therapy fails or structural cause present) Polypectomy / Myomectomy -- for polyp or fibroid. Endometrial ablation -- for refractory AUB in women not desiring fertility. Uterine artery embolization (UAE) -- for symptomatic fibroids. Hysterectomy -- definitive treatment when fertility not desired and other treatments have failed.

sub_questions.text: The pathogenesis of Acute Rheumatic Fever. [2]
sub_questions.answer: ARF is an autoimmune, non-suppurative sequela that follows Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis. Molecular mimicry: Antibodies generated against streptococcal cell wall proteins ( M proteins) cross-react with human tissues (heart, joints, skin, CNS), causing an inflammatory response. There is no single test to confirm the diagnosis. There is strong relationship with streptococcal infection and it is possible to prevent rheumatic fever by prompt treatment of streptococcal infection with penicillin.

sub_questions.text: The Criteria used for the diagnosis of Rheumatic Fever. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Diagnosis is based on the Revised Jones Criteria (2023 AHA guidelines) -- requires: Evidence of recent streptococcal infection (ASO titer ↑, throat swab, rapid antigen test) plus: 2 Major OR 1 Major + 2 Minor criteria

sub_questions.text: How will you treat a 13-year-old School going girl Lakshmi, who presented with Acute Rheumatic fever? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Treatment Eradicate streptococcal infection: Penicillin V orally for 10 days or IM Benzathine Penicillin G If penicillin allergy: Azithromycin or Erythromycin Anti-inflammatory therapy: Aspirin (60--100 mg/kg/day in divided doses) for arthritis Corticosteroids (e.g. Prednisolone) if moderate-severe carditis Supportive management: Bed rest Manage heart failure if present (diuretics, ACE inhibitors) Chorea: Valproate, Haloperidol, or Carbamazepine if severe

sub_questions.text: How will you prevent the recurrence of this conditon? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Prevention of Recurrence Secondary Prophylaxis (long-term antibiotic prophylaxis): Benzathine Penicillin G IM every 3--4 weeks; 12lac units (>30kg wt) ....6lac units ( <30kg wt) OR Penicillin V orally twice daily, 250 mg BD OR Erythromycin ( if penicillin allergy) , 250 mg OD Duration: 5 years or until age of 21 (whichever is longer) if no carditis 10 years or until age of 21 (whichever is longer) if carditis is present 10 years or until age of 40 ( whichever is longer) if carditis with valvular heart ds Educate the patient/family about early treatment of sore throat and importance of regular prophylaxis.

question_text: Define puerperium. What are the common problems of puerperium? [2+8]

sub_questions.text: Define puerperium. [2]
sub_questions.answer: Puerperium is the period following childbirth, typically lasting about 6 weeks (42 days), during which the maternal reproductive organs and physiology return to the non-pregnant state. It begins as soon as placenta is expelled . it is divided into immediate ( within 24hrs ) ; early ( upto 7 days) and remote ( upto 6wks). Includes physical, hormonal, and emotional adjustments. The no. of muscle fibres are no decreased but there is reduction in myometrial cell size. By end of 2wks uterus becomes a pelvic organ and then by 6 wks it is into prepregnant state. Vaginal discharge for first fortnight is called LOCHIA . Varoischanges also occure in urnary tract, gastrointestinal tract, wt loss, fluid loss, hematological changes.

sub_questions.text: What are the common problems of puerperium? [8]
sub_questions.answer: Puerperal Sepsis Infection of the genital tract occurring between rupture of membranes or labor and the 42nd day postpartum. Symptoms: Fever, foul-smelling lochia, pelvic pain, subinvolution of uterus. Secondary Postpartum Hemorrhage Bleeding occurring after 24 hours to 6 weeks postpartum. Causes: Retained placental fragments, infection, subinvolution. Breast Problems Engorgement: Painful swelling due to milk accumulation. Mastitis: Inflammation of breast tissue, often due to infection. Breast abscess: Localized pus collection, often requires drainage. Nipple fissures: Pain and cracked nipples, can hinder breastfeeding. Urinary Problems Urinary retention, incontinence, or UTI. Can result from trauma during delivery or catheterization. Bowel Problems Constipation: Common due to pain, dehydration, or reduced mobility. Hemorrhoids: May worsen post-delivery. Mental Health Issues Postpartum blues (common and mild). Postpartum depression or psychosis (require urgent attention). Thromboembolic Events Risk increased due to hypercoagulable state. Watch for signs of DVT or pulmonary embolism. Delayed Uterine Involution Uterus fails to return to pre-pregnancy size. May be associated with infection or retained products. Lactation Failure Inadequate milk production due to hormonal issues, stress, or poor attachment. Family Planning Needs Women may resume ovulation early; hence contraception counseling is important during puerperium.

question_text: A)Define Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM). [2] b) How will you manage a child with uncomplicated SAM? [3] c) What are the serious complications faced by children with SAM and how will you manage them? [5]

sub_questions.text: Define Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM). [2]
sub_questions.answer: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) is defined in children aged 6 months to 59 months as having any of the following: Weight-for-height/length z-score < −3 SD of the WHO growth standards. Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) < 11.5 cm. Presence of bilateral pedal edema of nutritional origin.

sub_questions.text: How will you manage a child with uncomplicated SAM? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Uncomplicated SAM means the child is alert, has appetite, no edema or infections, and can be managed as an outpatient. Management steps include: Nutritional Rehabilitation: Provide Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) such as Plumpy'Nut or homemade energy-dense food. Continue breastfeeding. Routine Medical Treatment: Antibiotics: Amoxicillin for 5--7 days. Deworming: Albendazole/Mebendazole as per age. Vitamin A supplementation and folic acid. Monitoring: Weekly follow-up to monitor weight gain (target: ≥5 g/kg/day). Assess for any complications or appetite loss.

sub_questions.text: What are the serious complications faced by children with SAM and how will you manage them? [5]
sub_questions.answer: Children with SAM are prone to several life-threatening complications, requiring inpatient care: Complication Management 1. Hypoglycemia Immediate feeding, 10% dextrose IV/NG tube feeding, monitor blood sugar. 2. Hypothermia Warm the child with blankets, room heating, skin-to-skin contact. 3. Dehydration Use ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition), avoid IV fluids unless in shock. 4. Electrolyte Provide potassium and magnesium supplements. Imbalance Avoid sodium-rich fluids. 5. Infections/Sepsis Empirical IV antibiotics: Ampicillin + Gentamicin. 6. Severe Anemia Blood transfusion if Hb < 4 g/dL or 4--6 g/dL with respiratory distress. 7. Anorexia or NG feeding if child is not eating. Appetite test Feeding Problems at admission. 8. Nutrient Give vitamin A, zinc, multivitamins. Avoid iron Deficiencies in initial phase.

Epiglottitis Sudden high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, toxic look, muffled voice, child sitting in tripod position 3. Foreign Body Sudden onset stridor, coughing, no fever Aspiration unless secondary infection develops, history of choking 5. Retropharyngeal Fever, drooling, neck stiffness, stridor, Abscess difficulty swallowing, muffled voice

sub_questions.text: Management of each of these conditions. [5]
sub_questions.answer: Condition Management 1. Croup (Viral) Mild: humidified air, oral dexamethasone (0.15--0.6 mg/kg). Moderate-severe: nebulized adrenaline + dexamethasone, monitor for respiratory distress. 2. Epiglottitis Emergency! Do not examine throat. Secure airway (intubation), IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone), ICU care. 3. Bacterial Airway management, suctioning, IV antibiotics Tracheitis (cloxacillin + cefotaxime), may need intubation. 4. Foreign Body Rigid bronchoscopy for removal. Supportive care. Chest Aspiration X-ray if history unclear. 5. IV antibiotics (clindamycin or ceftriaxone + Retropharyngeal metronidazole). sub_questions.text: How will you advice the parents regarding prevention and management of further episodes? [4]

sub_questions.answer: Adequacy of breast milk can be assessed clinically by checking if: Urine Output: Baby passes urine at least 6 times a day. Weight Gain: Baby gains weight appropriately (approx. 20--30 grams/day after first week). Feeding Pattern: Baby feeds 8--10 times a day, appears satisfied and sleeps between feeds. Stool Frequency: Yellow, seedy stools passed 2--4 times a day after first week. General Activity: Baby is alert, active, and not excessively crying or irritable.

sub_questions.text: How will you counsel her regarding proper feeding technique? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Counseling on Proper Breastfeeding Technique Positioning: Baby should be turned fully towards the mother ( abd of mother and baby are touching). Whole body is supported and not just neck. Head and body are in one line without any twist in neck. Baby's chin should touch the breast, and nose should be free. Mother should sit comfortably, supporting her back and arms. Attachment: Baby should take entire areola into the mouth, not just the nipple. Baby's chin touches breast. Lower lip should be turned out, mouth wide open. No clicking sound; swallowing should be audible. Frequency & Duration: Feed on demand, both day and night --- usually 8--10 times a day. Each feed should last 15--20 minutes per breast. Offer both breasts alternately. Confidence & Reassurance: Reassure that milk is produced in response to suckling. Discourage use of pre-lacteal feeds, bottles, or pacifiers.

question_text: A 20 year old lady, married 6 months back, now came with amenorrhea of 2 months duration and bleeding per vaginum since morning.

sub_questions.text: Mention the possible differential diagnoses? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Threatened abortion Inevitable/incomplete abortion Missed abortion Ectopic pregnancy Molar pregnancy (Hydatidiform mole)

sub_questions.text: Mention the clinical findings and investigations needed for evaluation of this lady to confirm the diagnosis. [3]
sub_questions.answer: Clinical Examination: General condition: Pallor, tachycardia, hypotension (suggestive of shock/ectopic). Abdominal exam: Tenderness, uterine size, guarding/rigidity. Per speculum exam: Bleeding, open/closed os, products of conception. Per vaginal exam: Uterine size, cervical status, adnexal tenderness or mass. Investigations: Urine pregnancy test -- To confirm pregnancy. Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) -- To confirm intrauterine/ectopic/molar pregnancy and viability. Serum β-hCG -- To correlate with gestational age or monitor falling/rising levels.

sub_questions.text: Briefly describe the management of each of your differential diagnoses? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Threatened Abortion: Conservative: Rest, avoidance of stress/intercourse. Progesterone support if indicated. Monitor bleeding and viability by ultrasound. Incomplete Abortion: Medical: Misoprostol to expel retained products. Surgical: Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) or D&C if excessive bleeding or incomplete expulsion. Ectopic Pregnancy: Medical: Methotrexate (if stable, early ectopic). Surgical: Laparoscopy/laparotomy if ruptured or unstable. Molar Pregnancy: Suction evacuation under ultrasound guidance. Monitor β-hCG levels weekly until negative and monthly thereafter for 6 months.

sub_questions.text: How will you counsel and follow-up this woman after treatment? [2]
sub_questions.answer: Counseling: Explain diagnosis and treatment undertaken. Emotional support for pregnancy loss. Emphasize importance of follow-up and future planning. Follow-Up: Regular β-hCG monitoring (especially in molar pregnancy). Advise contraception for 6 months in case of molar pregnancy or until β-hCG normalizes. Screen for anemia or infections. Address future fertility plans and preconception counseling.

question_text: Describe common neonatal problems. How to diagnose and manage each? As a Family Physician how will you educate mothers regarding new born care? [3+3+4]

sub_questions.text: Describe common neonatal problems. How to diagnose and manage each? [3+3]
sub_questions.answer: Neonatal Jaundice Yellowing of skin/sclera; confirmed by serum bilirubin. Management: Physiological jaundice: Monitor, ensure adequate feeding. Pathological jaundice: Treat underlying cause, phototherapy, exchange transfusion if needed. Neonatal Sepsis Poor feeding, lethargy, fever/hypothermia, respiratory distress; confirmed by blood cultures, CRP, CBC. Screening -- septic screen Definitive- blood culture Management: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin) + ceftriaxone if meningitis is suspected. Duration -- 1wk if on screening positive; 2wks if confirmed on culture; 3wks if CSF s/o meningitis. Hypothermia Axillary temp <36.5°C. Management: Warm environment, skin-to-skin care (kangaroo care), monitor temperature regularly. Adherence to the warm chain protocol. Devices used- radiant warmer or incubator. Hypoglycemia Blood glucose <40 mg/dL or plasma glucose < 45mg/dl in term neonates. C/F -- tremors , cyanosis, apathy, sweating, apnea, decrease feeding, stupor, convulsions. Management: Breastfeed early/frequently, IV glucose if symptomatic or very low levels. Detailed Mx discussed earlier Birth Asphyxia Poor cry/activity at birth, low Apgar score . Management: Immediate neonatal resuscitation, oxygen, supportive NICU care if needed.

sub_questions.text: As a Family Physician how will you educate mothers regarding new born care? [4]
sub_questions.answer: Breastfeeding: Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months. Early initiation (within 1 hour of birth), correct technique and frequent feeding (8--12 times/day). Warmth and Clothing: Keep baby warm, especially at night. Use skin-to-skin (kangaroo mother care) for low birth weight babies. Hygiene: Handwashing before handling the baby. Cord care: Keep it clean and dry, do not apply substances. Immunization: Explain the national immunization schedule. Encourage completion of vaccines on time. Danger Signs to Watch For: Poor feeding, convulsions, fever/hypothermia, difficulty breathing, jaundice before 24 hrs, no urine for >24 hrs. Follow-up: Schedule routine checkups. Monitor growth and development milestones.

question_text: One year old child is brought for check up with history poor development as compared to their previous child.

sub_questions.text: Define Development? What are the Rules of Development? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Development is a continuous, progressive process by which children gain skills and abilities in domains such as: Gross motor Fine motor Language Social and adaptive behavior Development refers to maturation of functions and acquisition of various skills for optimal functioning of an individual. Rules of Development: Cephalocaudal Rule -- Development progresses from head to toe (e.g., head control before walking). Proximodistal Rule -- Development progresses from central to peripheral (e.g., shoulder before fingers). Movements start as generalized and become more purposeful (e.g., random limb movement to grasping a toy). Development is a continuous process, startin in utero and progressing in an orderly manner until maturity. Development depends on functional maturation of nervous system Th sequence of attainment of milestones is the same in all children. Primitive reflexes have to be lost before relevant milestones are attained.

Monitor growth and development using developmental checklists at each visit. Promote responsive parenting -- encourage stimulation, play, talking, and early education. Support to the Family: Early referral to specialists (pediatrician, developmental therapist) for evaluation and intervention. question_text: A 55-year-old lady comes with vaginal discharge.

sub_questions.text: Describe the procedure of doing Pap's test. [5]
sub_questions.answer: Procedure of doing Pap's test (Papanicolaou smear) Preparation: Explain the procedure and obtain informed consent. Ensure the patient avoids intercourse, vaginal medications, douching or internal exams 24--48 hours before the test. Schedule the test mid-cycle (10--20 days after the first day of menstruation). Positioning: Position the woman in lithotomy position on an examination table. Speculum Insertion: Gently insert a sterile, warmed vaginal speculum to visualize the cervix. Sample Collection: Use an Ayre's spatula or cervical brush. Rotate 360° at the squamocolumnar junction (transformation zone). For liquid-based cytology, place the sample into the collection vial. For conventional smear, spread it evenly on a glass slide. Fixation and Labelling: Immediately fix the slide with a fixative spray or immerse in fixative. Label the specimen with patient details and send to the cytology lab.

question_text: A 27-year-old lady who is 8 weeks pregnant, presents to you with acute pain of the abdomen.

sub_questions.text: Discuss the differential diagnosis. [7]
sub_questions.answer: Obstetric Causes: Ectopic Pregnancy: Classic triad: amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, lower abdominal pain. May have adnexal tenderness or mass, cervical motion tenderness. Can rupture and cause hemodynamic instability. Threatened or Incomplete Abortion: Lower abdominal cramping with or without vaginal bleeding. Cervical os may be open in incomplete abortion. Molar Pregnancy: Abnormal uterine enlargement, severe nausea/vomiting, vaginal bleeding. May have passage of grape-like vesicles. Gynecological Causes: Ovarian Cyst Complications: Torsion or rupture of a corpus luteum cyst common in early pregnancy. Sudden severe unilateral pain, sometimes with nausea/vomiting. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (less common in pregnancy): Bilateral lower abdominal pain, fever, vaginal discharge. Cervical motion and adnexal tenderness. Non-Gynecologic Causes: Appendicitis: Right lower quadrant pain, nausea, fever. Uterus may shift the appendix slightly during pregnancy. Urinary Tract Infection / Pyelonephritis: Suprapubic or flank pain, dysuria, fever. Gastrointestinal Causes: Constipation, gastroenteritis, or biliary colic may present in early pregnancy.

sub_questions.text: How will you investigate the cause of the pain? [3]
sub_questions.answer: Pregnancy-related Tests: Urine Pregnancy Test or Serum β-hCG: To confirm intrauterine pregnancy and assess gestational age consistency. Serum Progesterone: Low levels may suggest nonviable pregnancy. Imaging: Transvaginal Ultrasonography (TVS): To assess intrauterine pregnancy, rule out ectopic gestation. Identify adnexal masses, corpus luteum cysts, or signs of molar pregnancy. Evaluate fetal viability (presence of fetal pole, cardiac activity). Others : CBC: To check for anemia (e.g., from bleeding), infection. Urinalysis: To rule out UTI. Blood Grouping & Rh Typing: If abortion or ectopic is suspected. CRP or ESR: If infection is suspected.

question_text: Discuss the methods of cervical cancer screening. [10]

sub_questions.text: Discuss the methods of cervical cancer screening. [10]
sub_questions.answer: Pap Smear (Conventional & Liquid-Based Cytology) Method: Cervical cells are collected using a spatula or brush and examined microscopically. Types: Conventional Pap smear: Cells are smeared on a slide. Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC): Cells are suspended in a liquid medium, improving specimen quality. Recommended Age: 21--65 years. Frequency: Every 3 years if normal (21--29 years). Every 5 years with HPV co-testing (30--65 years). Advantage: Detects cellular abnormalities (ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL). Limitation: Subjective interpretation; may miss glandular lesions. HPV DNA Testing Method: Detects high-risk HPV genotypes (e.g., HPV-16, 18) responsible for most cervical cancers. Used Alone or Co-tested with Pap smear in women ≥30 years. Advantages: Higher sensitivity for detecting high-grade lesions. Allows for longer screening intervals (every 5 years if negative). Limitations: Expensive; less accessible in resource-limited settings. Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) Method: Application of 3--5% acetic acid to the cervix, then visual inspection for acetowhite areas (indicating dysplasia). Used in: Low-resource settings. Advantages: Inexpensive, simple, immediate results. Can be done by trained paramedical staff. Limitation: Low specificity; higher false positives. Visual Inspection with Lugol's Iodine (VILI) Method: Application of iodine solution to the cervix. Normal cells stain brown, abnormal areas appear unstained (mustard yellow). Advantage: Better contrast than VIA. Limitations: Similar to VIA; not widely used alone. Colposcopy (Adjunct) Used as a diagnostic follow-up for abnormal Pap, VIA, or HPV test results. Magnifies cervical epithelium to guide biopsy.

question_text: A 50-year-old lady who attained menopause 2 years ago, has been coming to you for recurrent urinary tract infections. Outline the risk factors, clinical examination, investigations and management of recurrent UTI in this lady. [2+2+2+4]

sub_questions.text: Risk factors of UTI [2]
sub_questions.answer: Postmenopausal estrogen deficiency- Leads to vaginal atrophy and loss of lactobacilli, increasing colonization by uropathogens. Poor perineal hygiene or incontinence. Increased post-void residual urine- Due to age-related bladder dysfunction or prolapse. Diabetes mellitus- Impaired immunity and glycosuria promote bacterial growth. History of frequent antibiotic use - May lead to resistant organisms.

sub_questions.text: Clinical examination [2]
sub_questions.answer: General Examination Vitals (especially temperature). Signs of diabetes (skin infections, neuropathy). Abdominal Examination Palpate for bladder distention or tenderness. Pelvic Examination Look for: Signs of atrophic vaginitis. Pelvic organ prolapse (cystocele, rectocele). Urethral tenderness or discharge.

sub_questions.text: Investigations [2]
sub_questions.answer: Urine routine and microscopy Pyuria, bacteriuria. Urine culture and sensitivity To guide appropriate antibiotics. Blood glucose levels / HbA1c To rule out undiagnosed or uncontrolled diabetes. Ultrasound KUB (if indicated) Assess for residual urine, stones, or structural abnormalities.

sub_questions.text: Management [4]
sub_questions.answer: Acute Episode Treatment Empirical antibiotics (e.g. nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin) → adjusted based on culture. Adequate hydration and analgesia. Address Underlying Risk Factors Topical vaginal estrogen cream Improves urogenital flora and mucosal integrity. Control blood glucose if diabetic. Preventive Measures Encourage: Good perineal hygiene. Postcoital voiding. Increased fluid intake. Cranberry extract or D-mannose (limited evidence). Consider Urology Referral If structural abnormalities, recurrent pyelonephritis, or resistant infections are suspected.

question_text: Aetiology and assessment of dyspareunia. [5+5]

sub_questions.text: Aetiology of dyspareunia [5]
sub_questions.answer: Local/Genital Causes: Infections: Vaginitis (Candida, Trichomonas) STIs (Chlamydia, gonorrhea, herpes) Atrophic vaginitis (especially postmenopausal women) Vulvodynia or vestibulitis Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) Endometriosis Vaginal dryness or insufficient lubrication Structural causes: Vaginal septum, imperforate hymen, tight introitus, vaginal prolapse Psychological Causes: Anxiety, fear, history of sexual abuse Relationship conflict Body image issues or past trauma Musculoskeletal/Neurological Causes: Pelvic floor muscle hypertonicity or spasms Pudendal neuralgia Interstitial cystitis Post-surgical or radiation-related scarring After episiotomy, hysterectomy, pelvic surgeries, or pelvic irradiation

sub_questions.text: Assessment of dyspareunia [5]
sub_questions.answer: Detailed History: Location of pain: Superficial (introital) or deep (pelvic) Onset and duration: First intercourse vs. acquired Timing: During penetration, certain positions, or after intercourse Associated symptoms: Vaginal discharge, bleeding, urinary/bowel symptoms Menstrual history: Dysmenorrhea, irregular cycles Obstetric and surgical history Psychosexual history and mental health screening Physical Examination: External genitalia: Redness, lesions, ulcers, signs of infection or trauma Speculum exam: Vaginal walls, cervix, lubrication, discharge Bimanual exam: Uterine or adnexal tenderness (suggests PID or endometriosis) Pelvic floor exam: Check for muscle spasm/tenderness Investigations: Vaginal swabs and cultures Urine routine/microscopy Pelvic ultrasound (if deep pain suspected) STI screening

question_text: Clinical features and management of Bartholin's cyst. [5+5]

sub_questions.text: Clinical features of Bartholin's cyst [5]
sub_questions.answer: A Bartholin's cyst is formed due to obstruction of the Bartholin gland duct, leading to retention of gland secretions. Symptoms: Painless swelling in the posterior part of the vulva (usually unilateral) Discomfort while walking or sitting Dyspareunia (painful intercourse) Sometimes can be asymptomatic and discovered incidentally If infected (Bartholin abscess): pain, redness, warmth, and fever Signs: Swelling at the 5 o'clock or 7 o'clock position of the vaginal introitus Soft, fluctuant, and well-defined mass Overlying skin may be normal or inflamed if infected If abscess present: tender, warm, erythematous swelling with possible pus

sub_questions.text: Management of Bartholin's cyst [5]
sub_questions.answer: Asymptomatic : No treatment needed Advise hygiene and regular monitoring Symptomatict: Catheter insertion: After incision, a small balloon catheter is placed to keep duct open for 4--6 weeks Marsupialization: Surgical procedure to create a permanent opening for drainage Infected Cyst (Bartholin's Abscess): Incision and drainage (I&D) Word catheter or marsupialization after drainage to prevent recurrence Antibiotics if infection suspected or confirmed (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate or metronidazole) Analgesics and warm sitz baths Recurrent Cyst or Abscess: Excision of Bartholin gland and duct may be considered Postmenopausal Women: Cyst should be biopsied or excised to rule out malignancy (Bartholin gland carcinoma is rare but serious)

question_text: A 5-year-old girl is brought to you by her parents with the complaint that she has been dropping things lately. What history will you elicit if you suspect that the child has absence seizures? Briefly discuss the clinical examination, investigation and management of absence seizures. [3+3+2+2]

sub_questions.text: History to elicit for absence seizures [3]
sub_questions.answer: Episodes of sudden staring or unresponsiveness lasting for a few seconds~30secs. Often mistaken for daydreaming. Abrupt onset and termination of episodes, with no aura or no memory of the event. There is brief lapse of awareness or consciousness with discontinuation of of any activity being performed at that time. There is no loss of posture. Automatisms like lip-smacking, eye blinking, or hand movements during the event. Frequency of episodes (can occur many times a day). Triggers like hyperventilation or stress. Any relation to dropping objects -- may suggest a sudden loss of awareness. No urinary or stool incontinence Family history of epilepsy or similar episodes. Developmental history -- usually normal in typical absence seizures. Medical history -- prev sz / head injury/ infection / congenital issue. Social history -- sleep / screen time/ stress. Observation by teachers or caregivers . Any association with headache , nausea, vomiting , weakness, numbness , vision.

sub_questions.text: Clinical examination [3]
sub_questions.answer: Neurological examination: Typically normal in typical absence seizures. Developmental assessment: Check for developmental delay or regression. Hyperventilation test: Ask child to hyperventilate for 3--5 minutes -- may provoke an absence seizure. Rule out other seizure types: Observe for signs of myoclonic jerks or atonic seizures.

sub_questions.text: Investigations [2]
sub_questions.answer: EEG (Electroencephalogram): Classic finding: 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges during episodes. Provoked by hyperventilation. MRI brain (if atypical features): Only if neurological findings are abnormal or diagnosis is uncertain. CBC , serum electrolytes , RBS, LFT, KFT, toxicology , ecg Genetic testing , csf study .

sub_questions.text: Management [2]
sub_questions.answer: Medication: First-line: Ethosuximide (for typical absence seizures) Alternative: Valproic acid (if coexisting generalized seizures) Parental Education and Support: Reassure that many children outgrow absence seizures by adolescence. Emphasize adherence to medication and regular follow-up. Advise avoiding triggers (like sleep deprivation, hyperventilation).

question_text: A 2-year-old child is brought to you by his mother with a barky cough and shortness of breath from morning.

sub_questions.text: List the differential diagnosis. [2]
sub_questions.answer: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis) -- most common; viral etiology. E.g -- parainfluenza type 1,2,3 or RSV, adeno, rhino etc. Epiglottitis -- serious, with drooling and toxic appearance. Foreign body aspiration -- sudden onset, localized wheeze. Bacterial tracheitis -- high fever, toxic look. Allergic reaction/Anaphylaxis -- stridor, swelling, urticaria.

sub_questions.text: Discuss the clinical features, investigations, and management of croup. [3+2+3]
sub_questions.answer: Clinical Features Age: Typically 6 months to 5 years. History: Barky, "seal-like" cough. Gradual in onset Brassy cough Inspiratory stridor (worse when agitated or crying). With sternal recession Child anxious , restless Hoarseness of voice. Low-grade fever and preceding upper respiratory infection. Signs of respiratory distress: Tachypnea. Chest wall retractions. Nasal flaring in severe cases. Hypoxemia Cyanosis In severe cases -- silent chest. Investigations Usually a clinical diagnosis, but the following may be considered in unclear or severe cases: Neck X-ray (AP view): Classic "steeple sign" due to subglottic narrowing. Pulse oximetry: To assess oxygen saturation. Management Based on severity: Mild Croup (no stridor at rest): Single dose oral dexamethasone (0.15--0.6 mg/kg). Parental reassurance and home care. Moderate to Severe Croup (stridor at rest, respiratory distress): Nebulized epinephrine (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, max 5 mL) -- observe for rebound symptoms. Oral or IM dexamethasone -- anti-inflammatory action. Oxygen support if hypoxic. Hospitalization if persistent stridor or poor feeding/alertness. i/v fluids for dehydration neb with salbutamol & budecort injection MgSO4 or injection theophylline

question_text: A 4-year-old child is brought to you by his parents since he has been opening his bowels only once in 3 to 4 days. What further history would you elicit? What clinical signs would you look for? How will you manage constipation in this child? [3+2+5]

sub_questions.text: History to elicit for constipation [3]
sub_questions.answer: Stool Characteristics: Hard, dry, painful to pass Presence of blood or mucus Large diameter stools that may block the toilet Bowel Habits: Age at toilet training. Frequency and timing of bowel movements. Any fecal incontinence or soiling (suggestive of overflow) Dietary History: Fiber intake (fruits, vegetables). Fluid intake (water, juices, milk). Excessive dairy consumption (can worsen constipation) Psychosocial History: Stress (e.g., school, toilet avoidance) History of painful defecation leading to withholding behavior Associated Symptoms: Abdominal pain, bloating. Poor appetite, vomiting. Urinary symptoms (UTIs can co-exist). Red Flags (to rule out organic causes): Delayed passage of meconium at birth. Neurological issues (e.g., spina bifida, hypothyroidism). Weight loss or failure to thrive.

sub_questions.text: Clinical signs [2]
sub_questions.answer: Abdominal Examination: Distension or palpable fecal masses. Perianal Inspection: Fissures, tags (due to straining). Signs of withholding behavior. Soiling or overflow incontinence.

sub_questions.text: Management of constipation [5]
sub_questions.answer: Dietary Modifications Increase fiber intake (whole fruits, vegetables, cereals). Encourage adequate fluids (especially water). Limit excessive cow's milk (<500 mL/day). Behavioral Measures Establish regular toilet routine (especially after meals). Provide foot support while sitting to help effective straining. Use positive reinforcement (sticker chart, praise). Avoid English seat, use indian one . Pharmacological First-line: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) 3350 (with or without electrolytes) for disimpaction and maintenance. Alternatives: Lactulose, milk of magnesia. Duration: Continue maintenance therapy for several months to prevent relapse. Follow-Up and Monitoring Regular follow-up to assess stool pattern, medication side effects, and family adherence. Watch for signs of relapse or underlying organic causes.

question_text: Discuss the clinical features and management of acute otitis media in a 10 month old otherwise healthy child. Outline the role of delayed antibiotic therapy in this condition. [3+4+3]

sub_questions.text: Clinical features of AOM [3]
sub_questions.answer: In infants and young children, symptoms may be non-specific, but typical features include: Ear-related signs: Tugging or pulling at the ear Irritability or excessive crying Otalgia (ear pain) --- may present as disturbed sleep Systemic symptoms: Fever (may be high-grade) Poor feeding Vomiting or diarrhea (less specific) Signs on ear examination: Bulging, erythematous, opaque tympanic membrane Reduced or absent mobility of tympanic membrane on pneumatic otoscopy Possible middle ear effusion

sub_questions.text: Management of AOM [4]
sub_questions.answer: Pain Control (First-line): Paracetamol or Ibuprofen for fever and ear pain. Ensure adequate hydration and comfort measures. Antibiotic Therapy: Immediate antibiotics are indicated if: <6 months of age Severe symptoms (fever ≥39°C, otorrhea, toxic appearance) Bilateral AOM in children <2 years No improvement within 48--72 hours of observation First-line antibiotic: Amoxicillin 40--90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily × 5--7 days. If penicillin allergy: Azithromycin or Cefdinir. Supportive Care: Nasal saline drops for nasal congestion. Encourage breastfeeding or feeding for hydration.

sub_questions.text: Role of delayed antibiotic therapy [3]
sub_questions.answer: Also known as "watchful waiting", it is a valid approach in selected cases: Indications: Mild symptoms Age >6 months Unilateral infection Reliable caregivers who can follow up or start antibiotics if condition worsens Benefits: Reduces unnecessary antibiotic use Limits antibiotic resistance Allows spontaneous resolution (70--80% cases resolve without antibiotics) Implementation: Provide prescription but advise to use it only if: No improvement in 48--72 hours Symptoms worsen (more pain, fever, irritability)

question_text: A 6-month-old child was found to have a significant cardiac murmur when you saw her for an upper respiratory infection. An echocardiogram showed an atrial septal defect. Discuss the management of this condition. [10]

sub_questions.text: Management of Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) [10]
sub_questions.answer: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) is a congenital heart defect characterized by an abnormal opening in the atrial septum, allowing left-to-right shunting of blood. Types Ostium secundum (most common) -- Right axis deviation Ostium primum (associated with AV canal defects)- Left axis deviation Fossa ovalis Sinus venosus Coronary sinus defect History & Prognosis Small ASDs (<5 mm) may spontaneously close within the first 2 years. Larger ASDs may persist and cause complications such as: Right atrial and ventricular volume overload Pulmonary hypertension Arrhythmias later in life Stroke due to paradoxical embolism C/F- Often asymptomatic in infancy May present with: Recurrent respiratory infections Failure to thrive Poor weight gain On examination: wide fixed split of S2,delayed P2, systolic ejection murmur Fixed means no change with respiration Soft diastolic rumble X ray shows cardiomegaly, plethoric and prominent pulmonary artery. 2Decho -- RV enlarged. Intervention if - Size >8 mm with significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs >1.5:1) Evidence of right heart dilation on echo Symptomatic child (recurrent LRTIs, failure to thrive) Persistent large ASD beyond 2 years of age Management a) Conservative Indicated for small ASDs (<5 mm) in asymptomatic infants Regular follow-up with echocardiography every 6--12 months b) Medical Supportive Care Treat associated conditions like URTI, anemia, or heart failure if present Ensure nutritional support and monitor growth c) Surgical/Interventional Closure Timing: Usually after 2 years unless symptomatic earlier Methods: Device closure: Preferred for secundum ASDs with adequate rims (via catheterization) Surgical closure: Indicated when device closure is not feasible (e.g., very large ASD, rim deficiency, or non-secundum types) Parental Counseling Explain the nature of the defect and possible spontaneous closure Emphasize regular follow-up and timing of intervention Discuss excellent prognosis post-closure with near-normal life expectancy

question_text: A newly married couple comes to you for advice on delaying pregnancy.

sub_questions.text: Discuss the options that you will provide them. b) Describe Natural Family Planning methods.
sub_questions.answer: Options can be grouped into Temporary/Spacing Methods and Permanent Methods (though permanent methods are not advised for newly married couples). 1. Barrier Methods: Male Condoms: Easily available, no side effects Protect against STIs/HIV Requires proper and consistent use Female Condoms: Less commonly used Female-controlled barrier protection 2. Hormonal Methods: Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs): Taken daily Regularizes periods, reduces cramps Needs good compliance Emergency Contraceptive Pills (ECPs): For unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure Must be taken within 72 hours Injectables (DMPA): Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate One injection every 3 months May cause delayed return of fertility Contraceptive Patch / Vaginal Ring: Not widely available in India Similar to OCPs in hormone delivery 3. Intrauterine Devices (IUDs): Copper T (Cu-T): Effective for 5--10 years Can be removed anytime No effect on future fertility Hormonal IUD (LNG-IUS): Releases levonorgestrel Decreases bleeding and cramps 4. Natural Methods 5. Fertility Awareness & Counseling: Important to counsel about efficacy, side effects, availability, and mutual acceptability Offer couple-centered approach b) Natural Methods These involve identifying fertile days of the menstrual cycle and avoiding intercourse during those days. 1. Calendar (Rhythm) Method: Track menstrual cycles for 6--12 months Estimate fertile window: Start: Shortest cycle -- 18 days End: Longest cycle -- 11 days Avoid sex during fertile window 2. Cervical Mucus Method (Billings' Method): Assess changes in cervical mucus daily Clear, stretchy mucus = fertile phase Avoid sex during fertile mucus days and 3 days after peak mucus 3. Basal Body Temperature (BBT) Method: Measure body temperature every morning before getting out of bed Slight rise (0.5°F) after ovulation Abstain from sex from beginning of cycle until 3 days after temperature rise 4. Symptothermal Method: Combines BBT, cervical mucus, and other symptoms (breast tenderness, mid-cycle pain) for more accuracy 5. Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM): Effective up to 6 months postpartum if: Baby is exclusively breastfed Mother is amenorrheic Breastfeeds every 4 hours (day) and every 6 hours (night)

question_text: A 16-year-old girl visits your clinic and confides in you that she and her boyfriend have indulged in penetrative sex a few times.

sub_questions.text: What are the possible consequences of sexual contact at this age? b) How and what would be the content of your advice to the young girl?
sub_questions.answer: Engaging in sexual activity during adolescence can have physical, emotional, and social consequences: 1. Physical/Health Risks Unintended pregnancy Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) including HIV, HPV, chlamydia, gonorrhea Urinary tract infections (UTIs) or vaginal infections Menstrual irregularities due to stress or unprotected sex 2. sub_questions.answer: Increased frequency of urination in pregnancy may be physiological, but it can also indicate urinary tract infection (UTI) or gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). A clinical evaluation is essential. History: Onset, duration, and severity of symptoms Associated symptoms: Burning micturition, urgency → suggests UTI Excessive thirst, increased appetite, fatigue → suggests GDM Any fever, flank pain → indicates possible pyelonephritis Past history of UTI or diabetes Family history of diabetes Obstetric history: Any previous GDM, large baby, unexplained stillbirth, or polyhydramnios Examination: General: Look for dehydration, weight gain, BP (rule out preeclampsia) Abdominal exam: Uterine size appropriate for gestational age Urinalysis: Dipstick for glucose, ketones, and protein Microscopy for pus cells, bacteria (UTI) Fundal height (to assess for polyhydramnios in GDM) Investigations: 1. Urine Routine and Culture -- to rule out UTI 2. Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) -- to evaluate for GDM 75 g glucose, blood glucose measured at fasting, 1 hour, and 2 hours As per IADPSG or DIPSI criteria: Fasting ≥ 92 mg/dL 1 hr ≥ 180 mg/dL 2 hr ≥ 153 mg/dL → One abnormal value is diagnostic of GDM b) Discussed earlier

question_text: The mother of a 4-year-old girl says that her daughter has been suffering from repeated attacks of cold and cough over the past 6 months:

sub_questions.text: List the steps in the treatment of this case. b) Discuss the management of chronic suppurative otitis media.
sub_questions.answer: Recurrent cold and cough in a young child over months could be due to recurrent viral infections, allergies, asthma, enlarged adenoids, or underlying conditions like chronic sinusitis or immune deficiencies. Management involves a stepwise and holistic approach: 1. Detailed History and Physical Examination: Frequency and duration of episodes Presence of fever, wheezing, or ear discharge Environmental exposures (smoke, allergens, day-care attendance) Growth and development assessment Family history of atopy or asthma 2. Rule Out Specific Causes: Allergic rhinitis or asthma Tuberculosis (if prolonged symptoms or exposure) Reflux-related cough Immune deficiency (if frequent infections with poor recovery) 3. General Management: Reassurance: 6--8 mild viral infections/year is normal at this age Good nutrition, hand hygiene, avoidance of cold drinks/junk food Encourage regular physical activity and rest Avoid passive smoking exposure 4. Symptomatic Treatment: Saline nasal drops or sprays Steam inhalation Paracetamol for fever Antihistamines if allergic symptoms Antibiotics only if secondary bacterial infection is suspected (e.g. prolonged fever, purulent nasal discharge) 5. Investigations (if warranted): CBC, ESR Chest X-ray (if recurrent LRTI) Mantoux test/TB screening Ig levels if immune deficiency is suspected b) Discussed earlier

question_text: A 13-year-old girl is brought to you with a history of tiredness. On examination, you find that she is pale and undernourished.

sub_questions.text: What are the investigations that you will conduct? b) What are the prevention and treatment modalities for anemia in adolescents?
sub_questions.answer: To determine the type and cause of anemia, order the following: Hb - To confirm anemia and assess severity. Peripheral blood smear - To classify anemia (microcytic hypochromic → iron deficiency; macrocytic → B12/folate deficiency; normocytic normochromic → anemia of chronic disease). Serum ferritin / Serum iron / Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) - To assess iron stores and confirm iron deficiency. Reticulocyte count - To evaluate bone marrow response. Stool examination for ova/cysts - To detect hookworm or other parasitic infections. Urine routine and microscopy - To rule out chronic blood loss (e.g., hematuria or UTI-related). Serum Vitamin B12 and Folate (if macrocytic anemia suspected) C-reactive protein (CRP)/ ESR - To assess chronic inflammation or infection. b) Prevention: 1. Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (IFA): As per national guidelines (e.g., Weekly Iron-Folic Acid Supplementation -- WIFS Program): 100 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid once weekly for all adolescent girls (10--19 years). 2. Deworming: Albendazole 400 mg every 6 months to treat worm infestation. 3. Dietary Counseling: Promote iron-rich foods (green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates, eggs, meat, legumes). Improve intake of Vitamin C-rich foods to enhance iron absorption. Avoid tea/coffee with meals. 4. Menstrual Health Education: Address heavy menstrual bleeding as a contributor to anemia. 5. Health Education at Schools and Anganwadis: Focus on nutrition, personal hygiene, and anemia awareness. Treatment: 1. Mild to Moderate Iron Deficiency Anemia: Therapeutic oral iron therapy: Elemental iron 3--6 mg/kg/day in 2--3 divided doses. Continue for at least 3 months after Hb normalization to replenish stores. 2. Severe Anemia (Hb < 7 g/dL): May require parenteral iron therapy or blood transfusion depending on clinical status. 3. Treat Underlying Cause: Deworming, treating infections, improving nutrition. 4. Follow-up: Reassess Hb after 4--6 weeks and monitor response to treatment.

History: Nature, duration, and amount of bleeding Associated symptoms: pelvic pain, discharge, weight loss History of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) Past Pap smear/cervical cancer screening Risk factors: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, obesity, diabetes 2. Physical Examination: General examination for anemia, cachexia Abdominal and pelvic examination Speculum exam: inspect cervix for growths, polyps, ulcers Bimanual exam: assess uterine size and adnexal masses 3. Investigations: Transvaginal Ultrasound (TVS): Endometrial thickness >4 mm is suspicious Pap smear (if not up to date) Endometrial biopsy (via pipelle or D&C) Colposcopy and cervical biopsy if cervical lesion suspected Hysteroscopy if needed for direct visualization 4. Identify and Classify Cause: Atrophic endometrium (most common) Endometrial hyperplasia or cancer Cervical cancer Endometrial polyp or fibroid b) Cervical Carcinoma: Diagnosis and Treatment Diagnosis: Pap smear : Screening test for early detection of precancerous lesions Colposcopy + Directed Biopsy: Confirms presence and severity of lesion Staging (FIGO): Clinical staging based on pelvic exam, imaging (MRI/CT), cystoscopy, proctoscopy Staging is essential for treatment planning Treatment Modalities (Based on FIGO Stage): Stage Treatment Stage 0 Cryotherapy, LEEP, or conization (CIN) Stage IA1 Conization or simple hysterectomy Stage IA2 Radical hysterectomy + pelvic lymphadenectomy -- IB1 Stage IB2 Radical hysterectomy or concurrent chemoradiation -- IIA Stage IIB External beam radiation + brachytherapy + chemotherapy -- IVA (cisplatin-based) Stage IVB Palliative chemotherapy/radiation, supportive care Follow-up: Regular pelvic exams Pap smear or HPV testing as advised Counseling for symptoms of recurrence

question_text: A 24-year-old worker in an apparel manufacturing factory complains of irregular periods:

sub_questions.text: What are the causes for this condition? b) Describe the preventive steps that can be taken. c) Discuss the treatment modalities that are available.
sub_questions.answer: Causes of Menstrual Irregularities 1. Physiological: Stress (job-related, emotional) Excessive physical exertion or weight loss Obesity 2. Endocrine Disorders: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) -- most common in this age group Thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism) Hyperprolactinemia 3. Other Medical Conditions: Diabetes mellitus Anemia Eating disorders 4. Medications: Hormonal contraception Antipsychotics or antidepressants 5. Gynecological Conditions: Endometriosis Uterine fibroids Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) b) Prevention :- 1. Lifestyle Modifications: Maintain a healthy weight (BMI) Regular physical activity without over-exertion Adequate balanced diet (especially iron, protein, vitamins) 2. Stress Management: Relaxation techniques, counseling, adequate sleep Reducing workplace stress 3. Health Screening: Routine check-up for thyroid disorders, anemia, and diabetes Annual pelvic exam and Pap smear as per guidelines 4. Avoidance of Unnecessary Hormonal Use: Educate against overuse of emergency contraception or hormonal pills without medical advice c) Treatment :- 1. Specific to Cause: PCOS: Lifestyle changes, metformin, OCPs to regularize cycles Thyroid disorders: Thyroxine for hypothyroidism, antithyroid drugs for hyperthyroidism Hyperprolactinemia: Dopamine agonists (e.g., cabergoline) 2. Hormonal Therapy: Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) to regulate cycles Cyclical progesterone in cases of estrogen dominance 3. Iron and Nutritional Supplementation: For anemia due to heavy or irregular bleeding 4. Counseling and Support: Reproductive health education Address body image, eating habits, and emotional stress 5. Referral to Specialist: If no improvement with primary care management or if structural/anatomical cause is suspected

question_text: Elder abuse is becoming a common phenomenon:

sub_questions.text: What are the warning signs of this problem that you are likely to see in your practice? b) What are the preventive measures to prevent this issue? c) What are the legal remedies that are available to the elderly in such situations?
sub_questions.answer: Warning Signs of Elder Abuse 1. Physical signs: Unexplained bruises, cuts, burns, fractures, or repeated injuries Delay in seeking medical attention for injuries 2. Psychological signs: Fear, anxiety, withdrawal, depression, confusion Sudden changes in behaviour or reluctance to speak in front of caregiver 3. Neglect: Poor hygiene, dehydration, malnutrition Untreated medical conditions Unsafe or unsanitary living conditions 4. Financial abuse: Sudden loss of funds, missing belongings Unusual banking activities or changes in wills or property ownership 5. Social signs: Isolation from friends or family Restriction of visits or phone calls b) Prevention :- 1. Strengthening family and caregiver support: Encourage strong family bonds and regular communication Train caregivers in elder care and stress management 2. Community support and engagement: Promote day-care centres, elder self-help groups, senior citizen clubs 3. Routine screening by health workers: Use checklists during home visits or clinical evaluations Early identification of at-risk elderly 4. Awareness and education: Educate elders and families on their rights Promote awareness on elder abuse through community programs 5. Encouraging reporting mechanisms: Create safe, anonymous, and accessible ways to report abuse c) Laws :- 1. Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007: Legally mandates children or heirs to provide maintenance to senior citizens Elderly can approach the Maintenance Tribunal for monthly allowance 2. Protection under IPC : Sections dealing with assault, criminal intimidation, theft, or cheating can be invoked 3. Domestic Violence Act, 2005: Elderly women facing abuse in household settings are protected under this act 4. Helplines and Support Services: Senior Citizen Helpline (e.g., 14567 in India) NGOs and legal aid services for senior citizens 5. Police and Legal Aid: Senior citizens can file FIRs directly for abuse or neglect Free legal aid through District Legal Services Authorities (DLSA)

sub_questions.text: What is Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC)?
sub_questions.answer: Kangaroo Mother Care is a method of care for preterm and low birth weight (LBW) infants that involves continuous skin-to-skin contact between the baby and the mother (or caregiver), exclusive breastfeeding, and early discharge with adequate follow-up. Components: Skin-to-skin contact -- Baby is placed upright between the mother's breasts in direct skin contact. Exclusive breastfeeding -- Encouraged and supported. sub_questions.text: What could be causes of primary and secondary dysmenorrhea?
sub_questions.answer: Causes of Dysmenorrhea 1. Primary Dysmenorrhea Painful menstruation without identifiable pelvic pathology Common in adolescents and young women Caused by increased prostaglandin release → uterine contractions and ischemia Causes include: Idiopathic (most common) Prostaglandin-mediated uterine hypercontractility Psychological stress or low pain threshold 2. Secondary Dysmenorrhea Painful menstruation with an underlying pelvic pathology Onset is usually after age 25--30 years Common causes include: Endometriosis Chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, infertility, cyclical pain Adenomyosis Diffuse uterine enlargement, heavy bleeding, midline pain Fibroids (submucosal) Menorrhagia, pelvic pressure, irregular bleeding Pelvic Inflammatory Pelvic pain, fever, discharge, irregular Disease (PID) cycles IUCD-related Associated with crampy pain, especially with copper IUCD Cervical stenosis Obstructive symptoms, scanty bleeding, pain

sub_questions.text: Discuss the diagnosis and the initial management of dysmenorrhoea in this lady.
sub_questions.answer: Diagnosis History: Nature of pain (cyclical or continuous) Duration and location Associated symptoms: heavy bleeding, dyspareunia, infertility Use of IUCD, past surgeries, PID Examination: Abdominal/pelvic tenderness Uterine enlargement (adenomyosis) Adnexal masses (endometrioma, fibroid) Cervical motion tenderness (PID) Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: first-line for fibroids, adenomyosis, ovarian cysts CBC, CRP/ESR: rule out infection Urine pregnancy test: rule out ectopic pregnancy Further tests if needed: Diagnostic laparoscopy (for endometriosis) Vaginal swab if suspecting PID c) Mx of Dysmenorrhea 1. General Measures: Reassurance and education Regular exercise, adequate sleep, stress reduction 2. Medications: Type Drugs Notes NSAIDs Mefenamic acid, Ibuprofen, First-line for both primary Naproxen and mild secondary dysmenorrhea Hormonal Combined oral contraceptives Suppress ovulation and reduce Therapy (COC), progesterone-only pills endometrial proliferation Antibiotics If PID is diagnosed/suspected GnRH In confirmed endometriosis analogues (short-term) 3. Refer if - Severe cases not responding to initial therapy Suspected endometriosis, fibroids, adenomyosis requiring surgical evaluation

question_text: 40-year-old lady who has 3 children presents with history of urinary incontinence. She has urinary loss while coughing or sneezing, which is embarrassing her. Her deliveries were all vaginal, but prolonged. Discuss the diagnosis and management of her problem

sub_questions.text: Discuss the diagnosis and management of her problem
sub_questions.answer: Most likely diagnosis -Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI) Involuntary leakage of urine during increased intra-abdominal pressure such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or lifting. Pathophysiology: Weakening of the pelvic floor muscles and urethral sphincter support Often associated with multiparity, prolonged vaginal deliveries, obesity, and aging Other D/d's to Rule Out: Urge Sudden strong urge to urinate, inability to hold incontinence urine Overflow Constant dribbling due to overfilled bladder (e.g., incontinence neurogenic bladder) Mixed Combination of stress and urge symptoms incontinence History: Onset, duration, frequency of leakage Triggers (coughing, laughing, etc.) Fluid intake, bowel habits, parity and mode of deliveries Associated urgency or frequency Examination: Pelvic exam: Check for pelvic organ prolapse, atrophic changes Cough stress test: Ask patient to cough with a full bladder to observe for urine leak Assessment of pelvic floor tone Investigations - Urinalysis: To rule out UTI Bladder diary: Frequency and volume charting Pad test Ultrasound (if needed): Residual urine Urodynamic studies: If surgery is being considered or diagnosis unclear Management: 1. Conservative Treatment (First-line): Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises) -- strengthen pelvic floor Lifestyle changes: Weight reduction Avoid bladder irritants (caffeine, alcohol) Scheduled voiding 2. Medical Management: Topical estrogen (in postmenopausal women) -- improves urethral tone if vaginal atrophy present Duloxetine (SNRI) -- off-label, increases urethral sphincter tone 3. Surgical Options: Considered when conservative measures fail: Mid-urethral sling procedures (e.g., Tension-free Vaginal Tape - TVT) Colposuspension (e.g., Burch procedure) Bulking agents (less effective, temporary) Patient Education and Support: Reassure that this is common and treatable Encourage compliance with pelvic exercises Refer to a gynecologist or urologist if surgery is being considered

question_text: A 34-year-old married woman has come for antenatal checkup. You suspect that she may be having gestational diabetes.

sub_questions.text: Define gestational diabetes. b) How will you screen/ investigate for gestational diabetes in this lady? c) If she is found to have gestational diabetes, how will you manage her?
sub_questions.answer: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) is defined as: "Any degree of glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy." It typically develops in the second or third trimester due to insulin resistance caused by placental hormones. Blood glucose levels usually return to normal after delivery, but these women are at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life. b) Screening Whom to screen - Universal screening is recommended in India due to high prevalence. Risk factors: Age >25 years, obesity, family history of diabetes, previous GDM, macrosomia, PCOS. Between 24--28 weeks of gestation (or earlier if high risk). Screening Method (DIPSI method ): Single-step test: 75g oral glucose given regardless of fasting state. Measure plasma glucose 2 hours after ingestion. Interpretation (based on 2-hour value): ≥ 140 mg/dL → GDM < 140 mg/dL → Normal Alternative method (WHO criteria / 75g OGTT): Fasting: ≥ 92 mg/dL 1 hour: ≥ 180 mg/dL 2 hour: ≥ 153 mg/dL → Any one abnormal value confirms GDM. c) Discussed earlier

question_text: Child abuse is being more commonly seen in the newspapers. How would you screen for child abuse in your clinic? What are the available laws, systems to help victims of child abuse?

sub_questions.text: How would you screen for child abuse in your clinic? b) What are the available laws, systems to help victims of child abuse?
sub_questions.answer: Screen for Child Abuse A. History Taking (Red Flags): Inconsistent or vague history of injury Delay in seeking medical care Explanation of injury not matching developmental age (e.g., a 2-month-old "fell while running") Recurrent injuries or hospital visits History of emotional withdrawal, school performance decline B. Observation During Interaction: Child fearful or overly passive/aggressive Child flinches at touch or avoids eye contact Parent is overly aggressive or indifferent Poor hygiene, malnutrition, or inappropriate clothing C. Physical Examination: Bruises in protected areas (e.g., inner thighs, back, buttocks) Burns with clear demarcation (e.g., cigarette burns) Fractures in different healing stages Genital injuries, STIs (may indicate sexual abuse) Signs of neglect -- underweight, untreated infections D. Developmental or Psychological Indicators: Regression in developmental milestones Speech disorders or sleep disturbances Anxiety, depression, aggression, withdrawal 2. Available Laws and Systems A. Legal Framework (India): 1. POCSO Act, 2012 (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences): Deals specifically with sexual abuse and exploitation of children. Mandatory reporting for healthcare workers. Provides child-friendly procedures during investigation and trial. 2. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015: Addresses children in need of care and protection, including abuse victims. Institutional care, adoption, foster care provisions included. 3. Indian Penal Code (IPC): Sections like 323 (voluntarily causing hurt), 354 (outraging modesty), and 376 (rape) apply. 4. Right to Education Act, 2009: Prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment in schools. B. Reporting and Support Systems: Childline 1098 -- 24-hour toll-free helpline for children in distress. District Child Protection Units (DCPUs) -- Coordinate rescue, care, and rehabilitation. question_text: a) Describe the mode of action of intra-uterine contraceptive devices (IUCD). b) Discuss the optimum timing of insertion of IUCD.

sub_questions.text: Describe the mode of action of intra-uterine contraceptive devices (IUCD).
sub_questions.answer: Mode of Action of Intrauterine Contraceptive Devices (IUCDs) IUCDs prevent pregnancy by creating a local hostile environment in the uterus that interferes with sperm function, fertilization, and in some cases implantation. There are two main types of IUCDs: 1. Copper IUCDs (e.g., CuT-380A, CuT-375): Primary mechanism: Copper ions are toxic to sperm, reducing motility and viability → prevents fertilization Additional actions: Induce sterile inflammation of the endometrium, increasing leukocyte and prostaglandin production, which is spermicidal May also prevent implantation, although this is not the primary mechanism 2. Hormonal IUCDs (e.g., Levonorgestrel-releasing IUCD - LNG-IUS, Mirena): Primary mechanism: Releases levonorgestrel locally in the uterus Actions: Thickens cervical mucus → inhibits sperm penetration Suppresses endometrial proliferation → makes endometrium unsuitable for implantation In some users, inhibits ovulation partially

sub_questions.text: Discuss the optimum timing of insertion of IUCD.
sub_questions.answer: Optimum Timing of IUCD Insertion The timing depends on the woman's reproductive status and purpose of insertion: 1. Post-menstrual insertion (Interval IUCD): Best time: Within 7 days of menstruation onset Because , Cervical os is slightly open, ensures no early pregnancy, and minimal bleeding risk 2. Postpartum insertion: Can be done in institutional deliveries by trained person. Types: Immediate postpartum: Within 10 minutes after placental delivery Early postpartum: Within 48 hours after delivery Delayed postpartum: After 6 weeks if not inserted earlier Note: IUCD insertion between 48 hours and 6 weeks postpartum is generally not recommended due to increased risk of expulsion 3. Post-abortion insertion: After first trimester abortion: Immediately or within 7 days, if no infection After second trimester abortion: Usually deferred until 6 weeks, due to uterine size and risk of expulsion 4. Post-coital (Emergency) insertion: Within 5 days of unprotected intercourse Copper IUCD only is effective as emergency contraception

question_text: a) Define asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy. b) Why is active treatment for this advocated in pregnancy?

sub_questions.text: Define asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy.
sub_questions.answer: Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy is defined as: Presence of ≥10⁵ colony-forming units (CFU) of a single bacterial species per mL of urine in a clean-catch midstream specimen, in the absence of urinary symptoms (e.g., dysuria, frequency, urgency, fever). Confirmed on two consecutive specimens (especially in non-pregnant women), but in pregnancy, one positive culture is sufficient for diagnosis.

sub_questions.text: Why is active treatment for this advocated in pregnancy?
sub_questions.answer: Even though asymptomatic, ASB in pregnancy must always be treated due to serious potential maternal and fetal complications: Prevention of Pyelonephritis: ASB can progresses to acute pyelonephritis Pyelonephritis can cause maternal sepsis, preterm labor, and hospitalization Improves Pregnancy Outcomes: It is associated with preterm birth, low birth weight, and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) Treatment significantly reduces these risks High Risk Due to Physiological Changes: Pregnancy causes urinary stasis, vesicoureteral reflux, and immunological changes that predispose to infections Effective and Safe Treatment Options Available: Short courses of antibiotics like nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin, or cephalexin are effective and safe during pregnancy

question_text: a) How is asthma severity classified in children? b) List the medications and dosages in each grade of severity.

sub_questions.text: How is asthma severity classified in children?
sub_questions.answer: Asthma in children is classified based on frequency of symptoms, night awakenings, activity limitation, and lung function (if measurable). Classification varies slightly by age, but this is a general scheme for children ≥5 years (adaptable for younger ages): ✅ 1. Intermittent Asthma Daytime symptoms: ≤2 days/week Night-time symptoms: ≤2 times/month No interference with normal activity FEV1: Normal between episodes ✅ 2. Mild Persistent Asthma Daytime symptoms: >2 days/week but not daily Night-time symptoms: 3--4 times/month Minor limitation of activity FEV1 ≥80% predicted ✅ 3. Moderate Persistent Asthma Daily symptoms Night-time symptoms: >1/week (but not nightly) Some limitation of activity FEV1 60--80% predicted ✅ 4. Severe Persistent Asthma Symptoms throughout the day Frequent night-time symptoms (often nightly) Extreme limitation of activity FEV1 <60% predicted

sub_questions.text: List the medications and dosages in each grade of severity.
sub_questions.answer: Asthma treatment follows a stepwise approach, escalating or de-escalating based on control. Severity Step Medications Intermittent Step 1 - Low-dose ICS + SABA as needed or - SABA alone as needed (if very mild and infrequent) Mild Persistent Step 2 - Daily low-dose ICS (e.g., Budesonide 100--200 mcg BID) - SABA as needed Moderate Persistent Step 3 - Low-dose ICS + LABA (e.g., Budesonide 200 mcg + Formoterol 6 mcg BID) or - Medium-dose ICS alone Severe Persistent Step 4--5 - Medium- or high-dose ICS + LABA - Add LTRA (e.g., Montelukast 5--10 mg daily) - Refer to specialist - Consider oral corticosteroids in short bursts (e.g., Prednisolone 1--2 mg/kg/day for 3--5 days) Salbutamol (SABA) 100 mcg/puff (1--2 puffs via spacer, PRN) Budesonide (ICS) 100--400 mcg/day divided BID Fluticasone (ICS) 100--250 mcg/day divided BID Montelukast (LTRA) 5 mg once daily Prednisolone (oral) 1--2 mg/kg/day × 3--5 days (max 40 mg/day) LABA (Formoterol) 6 mcg BID (only in combination with ICS) Inhaled medications should be given via spacer

sub_questions.text: List 4 common skin infections in childhood.
sub_questions.answer: Four Common Skin Infections in Childhood 1. Impetigo 2. Scabies 3. Tinea (Dermatophytosis) 4. Molluscum Contagiosum

sub_questions.text: Describe clinical features and management of each of the above.
sub_questions.answer: 1. Impetigo Etiology: Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes Types: Non-bullous (common) and bullous Clinical Features: Begins as red papules → progress to honey-colored crusted lesions Common on face, around nose and mouth Highly contagious; may cause local lymphadenopathy Management: Local hygiene: Wash with soap and water Topical antibiotics: Mupirocin or fusidic acid for limited lesions Oral antibiotics (if extensive): Cloxacillin, Cephalexin Keep nails short to prevent autoinoculation 2.
